Iranian parliamentary committee approves fees on ships using Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:15:49 UTC
04:15:49 KST

The Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee has approved a provision in a draft law allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The official IRNA news agency said on Sunday that the committee continued its review of the proposed “Strategic Action Plan to Ensure the Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said members approved Article 3 of the bill after its consideration was postponed at a previous meeting.
The provision allows fees to be charged for navigation and environmental services, fuel supplies in special cases, insurance, security and other services provided in the strait, he said.
Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency designated by Tehran.
He maintained that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait of Hormuz.
The text recognises freedom of maritime navigation under international law and regulations while emphasising respect for the security and sovereignty of coastal states and the protection of their rights, he added.
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major sticking point in efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
Before the war, there was free passage through the strait, a critical export route for Gulf oil and gas, but Iran now insists on retaining control and charging fees, something the US rejects.
Legislative process
For the proposal to become law in Iran, the relevant parliamentary committee must first debate and approve its provisions.
The committee’s report is then submitted to the full parliament, which votes on the individual provisions and the bill as a whole.
If passed, the legislation is referred to the Guardian Council to determine whether it complies with the Constitution.
Any objections would send the bill back to parliament, while the Expediency Council could intervene if the dispute remains unresolved.
Once approved by the Guardian Council, the legislation is promulgated by the president and enters into force.

His move is expected to swiftly see his partner Lea Salame, a top newsreader on TF1’s rival France 2 public TV, to announce that she is stepping aside to avoid any conflict of interest in the presidential campaign.
Glucksmann emphasised he was not part of “classical political” circles, referring to his past work abroad in the aftermath of genocide in Rwanda and as a former adviser to the anti-Moscow former Georgian president Mikheil Saakashvili.
Now in jail in his home country, Saakashvili was a staunch foe of Russia after the 2008 war between the two nations.

Far-right figurehead Marine Le Pen scents her best ever chance of winning the race for president.

Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is planning to stand while Greens leader Marine Tondelier is campaigning while pregnant.
Socialist Party (PS) leader Olivier Faure and even possibly ex-president Francois Hollande are also mulling runs.
Polls give Glucksmann, who’s popular among young people in what some term “Glucksmania”, 10-12 per cent of the vote, a creditable score but likely not enough to make a second round run-off.

He confirmed he would take part in the primary with my “Socialist friends” and added: “We will win this presidential election, I am convinced.”
“I am a candidate to win and to change France,” he said.
Besides being a staunch European who abhors the far right, Glucksmann is a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion.
He acknowledged having “long discussions” with Salame, “as in any couple when the decision of one person has such an impact on the life of another”.
“I know what this decisions means for my loved ones and in particular my partner,” he said.
Beirut-born Salame, 46, had already acknowledged she would step aside from her job presenting the flagship news show she has held since 2025 if her partner stood for president.
But she has insisted she remains objective.
“I am an independent, honest journalist – a free woman,” she said in February, while acknowledging questions about their personal and professional situation were “legitimate”.
A source close to her channel, asking not to be named, said Salame was expected to officially announce her decision in the next hours. AFP

'I shouldn't be here': Australian murder suspect speaks from Thai prison for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:12:46 UTC
04:12:46 KST

Accused murderer Simon Carman says he fought Thai teenager in self-defence
In short:
The Perth man accused of murdering a 17-year-old girl in Thailand after picking her up in Pattaya says he is innocent and acted in self-defence.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, talked to the ABC in his first media interview since his arrest in late June.
What's next?
Pattaya police have concluded their investigation and intend to pass the case to prosecutors today.
Simon Peter Carman, the Australian man charged with murdering Thai teenager Tunchanok Donhomla, says he acted in self-defence to stop her from stabbing him.
The 45-year-old spoke exclusively to the ABC's Foreign Correspondent program in a private visitors' room at Pattaya Remand Prison, where he has been detained for almost two months.
"I'm hoping and praying that I get released," he said.
"I have not done anything wrong. I shouldn't be here … I do not understand what's going on."
Thai police have accused Mr Carman of picking up the 17-year-old along Pattaya's popular Beach Road in the early hours of June 25, then killing her and discarding the body.
In a 30-minute interview, conducted under the close watch of a prison guard, Mr Carman said he was innocent and did not intend to kill the teenager.
"I feel deeply sad. I obviously wish it never happened, but it was unavoidable," he said.
"All I was trying to do was restrain her from stabbing me."
The ABC is the first foreign news organisation in at least 15 years to receive permission to interview a foreign inmate in a Thai prison. The interview was permitted on the condition that prison officials could review the ABC's footage for security reasons, and that prison conditions were not discussed. The interview was carried out with Mr Carman's consent.
He faces four charges, including murder, concealing a corpse, and abducting a minor for indecent purposes.
If found guilty of murder, he faces the death penalty or life in prison.
"I pled not guilty, and I remain not guilty of all four charges," Mr Carman said.
Mr Carman told the ABC he did not have a lawyer yet and had not received any visitors apart from Australian embassy officials.
Thai police wrapped up their investigation last week and intend to pass the case to prosecutors today.
Tunchanok Donhomla's father, Thongchai Donhomla, said he wanted Mr Carman to receive a life sentence or the death penalty to "serve as a lesson for others".
"I want Simon to receive the harshest punishment because I have lost my child," he told the ABC in an interview last week.
Carman says pair fought over money
Ms Tunchanok, known affectionately by her friends and family as "Cake", was last seen alive on June 25.
CCTV captured her walking hand in hand with Mr Carman into the elevators of his condo building.
Loading...
It later captured Mr Carman dragging a large suitcase out of the building and transporting it on a motorcycle at night.
Two days later, police found Ms Tunchanok's body in the suitcase, which had been dumped along railway tracks near Mr Carman's accommodation.
Mr Carman was arrested at Bangkok's international airport on June 27 while trying to board a flight to Perth, and has been in Thai police custody since.
In the interview with Foreign Correspondent, Mr Carman maintained he had acted in self-defence.
Mr Carman said he first met Ms Tunchanok on the street, where she was accompanied by two friends. He said the 17-year-old then followed him back to his accommodation.
"I honestly do not know why she followed me home," he added.
When the ABC told him there was CCTV showing them entering the building holding hands, Mr Carman said: "I cannot remember that, but if it was hand-in-hand, I believe you."
He said he was not aware Ms Tunchanok was a minor at the time, and believed she was roughly 25 to 35 years old.
Mr Carman said when they got to his room he "gave her 500 baht ($21) … for nothing. And she wanted more money and then she pulled a knife".
He said he repeatedly asked Ms Tunchanok to "put down the knife" during a physical struggle, and that eventually "she went limp".
When asked if he had called anyone, including an ambulance, Mr Carman said he had not because he "didn't trust the police".
Family 'deeply heartbroken' by case
Pattaya Police Colonel Anek Srathongyoo said his investigation team would submit its case file to the Pattaya prosecutor's office today.
Prosecutors will then have until September 18 to indict Mr Carman.
"The autopsy report said that Cake had a brain injury and she suffocated. She had no other injuries," Colonel Anek told the ABC last week.
"We also collected Simon [Carman's] DNA and matched it to DNA found on Cake's body."
Ms Tunchanok's father told the ABC he was "deeply heartbroken" by the case.
"I always told my child to be a good person, never to cheat or harm anyone. But if a bad situation happens, I always told her never to back down to anyone and to fight to the very end," Mr Thongchai said.
"I don't ask for much. I just hope my child gets the justice she deserves."

Every Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city about $12 million. They now come almost twice in week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:10:14 UTC
04:10:14 KST

Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. Russian strikes have already damaged more than four thousand buildings in the capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in answer to a Novyny.LIVE journalist.
Russian forces now strike Kyiv with ballistic and cruise missiles or drones on average almost twice a week. The latest massed attack, on the night of 20 August, killed at least 16 people in Kyiv and the region.
The cumulative damage keeps growing
The toll on the city's housing is vast. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, Klitschko continued, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.
New shelters are planned, but old money went unspent
Kyiv plans to expand its shelter network. By the end of 2026, the city intends to install new mobile shelters, placed first in districts and locations that lack other accessible cover, Klitschko stated.
The plan follows a failure that the mayor acknowledged. Last year, Kyiv allocated $12 million for mobile shelters, but the district administrations did not use the money. It was returned to the city budget.
The capital also still lacks enough professional bomb shelters capable of better protecting people during missile strikes, he added. This gap persists as tens of thousands of Kyiv residents shelter in metro stations through the attacks.
The city is building a backup heating system
Meanwhile, Kyiv is preparing for winter under fire. The city has completed more than 50% of planned work to create a backup heating system, with readiness at some sites already reaching 90%, the Kyiv mayor added.
Russia has struck Ukraine's energy and heating infrastructure each winter of the war. A backup system is Kyiv's insurance that a successful strike on one heat source does not leave districts frozen, part of the same preparation for the heating season that Ukraine's government is racing to complete nationally before the cold.

The EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to Serbia because of large-scale fires
Kyiv • UNN
The EU has sent Serbia four helicopters, 124 firefighters and equipment to fight forest fires. The blaze has engulfed the Deliblato Sands and other areas.
On Saturday, the head of the EU mission in Belgrade stated that the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism had sent helicopters and firefighters to assist Serbia in combating a large-scale forest fire in a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Serbia activated the mechanism on Friday after several weeks of battling a forest fire in the Deliblato Sands, a unique site combining sand dunes and forests located approximately 80 km from the capital, Belgrade, as well as other fires in the southwest of the country.
"We are supporting Serbia in protecting lives, livelihoods and the unique natural heritage of the Deliblato Sands," Andreas Beckkerat, head of the EU mission in Belgrade, wrote in his message.
Luka Čaušić, head of Serbia's emergency management department, said that the European assistance included four Black Hawk firefighting helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic; 55 firefighters and 24 pieces of equipment from Germany; as well as 69 firefighters and 15 pieces of equipment from Romania.
On Saturday, one helicopter from Romania and one from Slovakia joined the firefighting efforts, while the other two from the Czech Republic will be deployed on Sunday, according to a statement from Serbia's Ministry of Internal Affairs.
Romanian firefighters and equipment also arrived in the town of Bela Crkva, located near the fire site. The German team is expected to arrive on August 24, the statement said.
In addition
Serbia is not an EU member, but it has access to emergency assistance from the EU under its Civil Protection Mechanism.
This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and an emergency response team to assist Spain in combating forest fires after repeated fires across Europe depleted the EU's resources.
On Wednesday, a Russian Il-76P firefighting aircraft belonging to the Ministry of Emergency Situations landed in the southern Serbian city of Niš to fight a forest fire that has destroyed thousands of hectares of pine forest since late July.
Čaušić said that the situation had stabilized on Saturday, but strong winds were expected, and the priority was to protect populated areas and human lives.

Iranian parliamentary committee approves fees on ships using Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:04:22 UTC
04:04:22 KST

Mustafa Melih Ahishali, Muhammet Torunlu and Rania Abushamala
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
 The Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee on Sunday approved a provision in a draft law allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The official IRNA news agency said the committee continued its review of the proposed “Strategic Action Plan to Ensure the Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said members approved Article 3 of the bill after its consideration was postponed at a previous meeting.
The provision allows fees to be charged for navigation and environmental services, fuel supplies in special cases, insurance, security and other services provided in the strait, he said.
Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency designated by Tehran.
He maintained that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait of Hormuz.
The text recognizes freedom of maritime navigation under international law and regulations while emphasizing respect for the security and sovereignty of coastal states and the protection of their rights, he added.
 
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major sticking point in efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
 
Before the war, there was free passage through the strait, a critical export route for Gulf oil and gas, but Iran now insists on retaining control and charging fees, something the US rejects.
Legislative process
For the proposal to become law in Iran, its provisions must first be debated and approved by the relevant parliamentary committee.
The committee’s report is then submitted to the full parliament, which votes on the individual provisions and the bill as a whole.
If passed, the legislation is referred to the Guardian Council to determine whether it complies with the Constitution and Islamic principles.
Any objections would send the bill back to parliament, while the Expediency Council could intervene if the dispute remains unresolved.
Once approved by the Guardian Council, the legislation is promulgated by the president and enters into force.

Landslide at Guinea landfill kills 30
CONAKRY – A landslide at a landfill in Guinea’s capital killed 30 people, the government said on Aug 23, after heavy rains overnight prompted the collapse of a massive mound of waste that engulfed nearby tents and shacks.
The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the ongoing rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
The landslide took place at around 2am local time in the Gbessia commune of Conakry, according to a government statement. The death toll was 30, with six people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.
Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.
One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.
Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November.
But the West African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than US$4.20 (S$5.30) per day, according to a World Bank report published in April.
Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djenab Toure, announced on Aug 20 that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to be relocated outside Conakry.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the landfill on Aug 23 to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

The AI sleeper issue that could sway Australian elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
At the last federal election, Tim Wilson won back the seat of Goldstein by 175 votes. The LNP held Longman by 269 votes, and in Bradfield, 26 votes determined who went to Canberra.
Those numbers gave the competing candidates an extraordinary white-knuckle ride.
We've all heard about the risk of deepfakes, misinformation campaigns and foreign interference meddling in elections and compromising democracy, but what if the more seismic change at the next election isn't just the usual flood of misleading material on social media?
A study published in Nature in December tested voters during elections in the United States, Canada and Poland. Participants had conversations with AI chatbots instructed to advocate for particular candidates.
The conversations shifted voters' political preferences. In some of the experiments, the effect was larger than that typically produced by conventional political video advertising.
AI persuaded people with arguments, facts and evidence, but not all those facts were accurate.
These conversations weren't with union members campaigning for Labor or die-hard Liberals out on the hustings making the case about debt and deficit.
It matters because voters have no clear way of knowing what sources are being included or excluded from the answers people are getting.
The sleeper issue is not about shifting millions of voters to influence an election result. Looking at marginal seats at the state and federal level, only a few hundred voters can make a difference.
AI's impact on voters
Victoria votes on November 28 and recent polling by RedBridge suggests around 8 per cent of Victorian voters remain undecided even after being pushed to say which way they lean.
At the last state election, Labor held Bass by 202 votes. There is no evidence AI had anything to do with that result.
Australia now has the conditions that make AI's impact on politics go from academic to reality, with undecided voters, seats with tiny margins and growing evidence that AI can persuade people.
More Australians are also increasingly turning to AI for information. University of Canberra research this year found 9 per cent of Australians used AI chatbots for news. Among 18- to 24-year-olds, it is 16 per cent.
The Victorian election will be a live test in Australia for where voters use AI to work out what politicians are offering.
Instead of searching through policies, news stories and candidate websites, one prompt in an AI chatbot can spit out which party it says has the best housing policy, what new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll will do about crime, or where Jess Wilson and the Liberals stand on health spending.
Treating AI like Google might sound useful, in particular to cut through all the political spin and advertising, but in an effort to find the truth, AI could also offer plausible, confident but incorrect advice.
Risk goes beyond ads
Independent MP Zali Steggall has a bill to crack down on deceptive political advertising and AI in politics. The bill would establish a political advertising standards board, require political advertising to comply with an enforceable ethical code, and require content substantially created through AI to carry a watermark.
Those are real risks she has identified, but they involve information being pushed at voters.
Political ads flood websites and TV screens, but someone at home asking AI who to vote for slips through the cracks. It is hard to imagine any laws, however well designed, being capable of catching this — and the impact of this is barely on the political radar.
The Australian Electoral Commission has started to look more closely at what AI chatbots tell people about federal election processes.
But who is actually in charge of overseeing this and how it affects our electoral system isn't clear.
The Victorian Electoral Commission is already warning about the use of generative AI in campaign material.
But the rules are still largely built around somebody producing political material and sending it to voters. The harder issue comes when the voter starts a conversation with AI.
The ABC's Vote Compass shows the standard of accountability we expect. It has a methodology. The basis for the comparison is transparent. And it does not tell people who to vote for.
A voter can now ask AI to perform something similar in seconds, but there is no clear way to know how it reaches the answer.
Loading
Voters need trustworthy information
Before the Dutch election last year, the country's privacy regulator tested major AI chatbots as voting advisers.
The recommendations were heavily concentrated around a small number of parties, even though the voter profiles covered a much wider political spectrum.
That did not prove deliberate partisan bias, but it showed the systems were capable of reducing a complicated political contest to a narrow, click-through set of recommendations.
Victoria has Labor and the Coalition, but also the Greens, One Nation, independents and minor parties fighting for votes.
AI makes propaganda cheaper and much easier to produce at scale, but concentrating on foreign actors misses our blind spot.
An AI model doesn't need to be hacked to be wrong.
Voters can make whatever choice they want. But they deserve to know whether the advice they get is based on credible information or an opaque system working on assumptions that can't be properly tested.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

====================================================================================================

Climate change and corruption are also driving up interest rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
As Paul Keating would say, the pet shop galahs are talking about the reason long-term interest rates are surging: the competing demands for money from big-spending governments and AI companies.
All other borrowers are getting trampled as the two bond-issuing elephants compete for cash.
But there are two other things the galahs should consider: corruption and the weather.
I'll get onto those in a minute, but first, let's talk about elephants — and the bond vigilantes, who flexed their muscles last week.
As the US government's debt mountain hit $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) on Tuesday, the bond market started charging 5.3 per cent for its 30-year money, the highest since 2007.
At about the same time, Australian government debt hit $1 trillion, and its 30-year bond rate went to 5.6 per cent for the first time (these only started being issued 10 years ago).
But these were two very different debt milestones: the American economy is 16 times Australia's, but its government debt is 56 times ours.
And Australians don't care as much about bond rates as Americans do because our mortgages are mostly variable rate, set by the RBA cash rate; in the US, most mortgages are 30-year fixed rate, and the interest rate is set to the 30-year bond.
The US government is now forking out $US1.2 trillion a year on interest, which is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent acted last week, buying both 10- and 30-year bonds to drive the prices up and the interest rates down.
It worked, briefly: the 30-year rate dropped from 5.33 to 5.19 per cent, but by Friday it was back at 5.25 per cent because markets understood that Bessent had just moved some deck chairs on the ship steaming towards an iceberg.
To raise the cash to buy those bonds, Treasury had to issue shorter-term ones, so neither the amount of debt changed nor the budget deficit that keeps adding to it.
Loading...
Something structural this way comes
Bond rates rise when an economy is doing well, and it looks like inflation is moving up.
But while inflation is part of the story this time, it's only a small part. This time something much deeper and more structural is going on, two things, in fact.
First, government budgets have been deteriorating for decades, and although there was an effort to reduce deficits after the GFC, that didn't happen after the COVID pandemic.
Second, the global corporate sector is in the midst of one of the greatest capital-raising programs in history, building the computing power needed for AI.
It's greater than the railroad building of the 19th century, the electrification of the first half of the 20th century, and the telecommunications infrastructure of the second half.
Whether the revenue from AI will justify the spending is unknown; probably it won't, but for the moment, the spending is soaking up global savings at the same time as governments are doing the same.
Meanwhile, trust in all institutions, including governments, is in decline, in tech companies as protests break out over data centres on top of anxiety about the impact of AI, and in governments, because of corruption.
Transparency International has just released its corruption perception indices for 2025, and it's getting worse almost everywhere, including Australia, down from 10th to 12th place.
The United States is ranked 29th and is now seen as one of the most corrupt developed countries in the world, beaten only by Spain, Italy, Greece and Portugal.
The corruption perception indices are also rising steeply in the United Kingdom, with some deterioration in Canada, New Zealand, France and Ireland.
What's going on?
Faith in public finances declining
The perception of corruption is correlated to polarisation and inequality, which are also rising everywhere, nowhere more than in America.
The latest report from the think tank that measures democracy and polarisation, V-Dem, says: "The US democracy is currently in a much faster deterioration process than any other democracy in modern times."
In just the past year, the US's score on the V-Dem Liberal Democracy index has declined by 24 per cent, and its world ranking dropped from 20th to 51st place out of 179 nations.
Last week the former editor, and now editor at large of the Wall Street Journal, Gerard Baker, a man not known for being left-wing or anti-corporate, wrote an op-ed that contained this long and surprising (for him) sentence:
"The widespread popular dissatisfaction with the working of modern American capitalism may be the product of some real, objective problems in the way American capitalism is working: income and wealth inequality on a scale not seen in a century; the concentration of economic, cultural and increasingly political power in a class of technology leaders whose products are dissolving the bonds that keep society together; the tightening nexus between business elites and the people who control the political process; rampant corruption and a political establishment that doesn't seem interested in accountability; the revival, after decades of stable prices, of inflationary pressures that are pushing the cost of living to painful levels."
He added: "Most of the causes of America's economic dysfunction are the result of a capitalism that has mutated into a system run by and for large corporate interests."
Bond investors might not talk about corruption and political polarisation because they tend to be part of the system Baker is calling out, but faith in public finances declines as perceptions of corruption rise, and that, in turn, drives up credit risk and interest rates.
Loading
Climate costs will dwarf AI
As for the weather, 2026-27 looks like being a double whammy: the most brutal El Niño since 1983 on top of the hottest year on record because of climate change.
The Southern Oscillation Index, which measures El Niño events via air pressure anomalies between Tahiti and Darwin, is at minus 29.1, the lowest since it reached minus 33.3 in February 1983.
The 1982-83 El Niño resulted in Australia's worst ever drought, a collapse in agricultural production, a massive dust storm in Melbourne, and above all the horrendous Ash Wednesday bushfires on February 16, 1983, in which 75 people died, and 2,545 families lost their homes.
Meanwhile, scientists have detected a sharp acceleration in the pace of global warming, which is behind the horrendous fires in Europe this northern summer.
This year looks like being the hottest year on record, with the global average temperature already reaching the 1.5 degrees of warming that was the maximum everyone agreed at the Paris climate conference in 2015.
This academic paper published in March reported that global warming has accelerated. The plain language summary says:
"In this study, we subtract the estimated influence of El Niño events, volcanic eruptions and solar variations from the data, which makes the global temperature curve less variable, and it then shows a statistically significant acceleration of global warming since about the year 2015. Warming proceeding faster is not unexpected by climate models, but it is a cause of concern and shows how insufficient the efforts to slow and eventually stop global warming under the Paris Climate Accord have so far been."
According to the Climate Action Tracker, current policies in place around the world are projected to result in about 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming above pre-industrial levels.
If the long-term or net zero targets agreed at Paris are included (that is "pledges and targets" not actually adopted yet), warming would be limited to between 2.2C and 2.4C.
All those temperatures would be various degrees of catastrophic … and expensive, for governments, companies and households.
APRA's recent "Insurance Climate Vulnerability Assessment" estimated that with 1.8C of warming, 26 per cent of Australian households won't be able to afford insurance by 2050.
That's a million more than are uninsured now, and that's only with 1.8C, which we're not far off.
The capital, savings and government debt required to pay for flood, fire and cyclone damage, not to mention a more urgent effort to cut carbon emissions, will make the AI investment boom and current government deficits seem like a snack.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

====================================================================================================

Labore: Social security cuts push nearly 100,000 more people into low income
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:58:32 EEST
03:58:32 KST

Tax and social security changes introduced by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s government have left nearly 100,000 more people on low incomes than under Finland’s previous system, according to a study by the Labour Institute for Economic Research Labore.
The study found that unemployed people, low-paid workers and employees working part-time have borne much of the impact.
Researchers Merja Kauhanen and Milla Nyyssölä compared the tax and benefit system in force in April 2026 with the 2023 system, using the same 2026 population data.
Their microsimulation found that about 99,000 more people live in low-income households under the current system than would have done so if the 2023 rules had remained in place.
The changes have also affected people who combine employment with social security benefits. Labore estimated that the number of employed people living in low-income households is about 28,000 higher under the April 2026 system.
Recipients of adjusted unemployment benefits, which allow unemployed people to combine earnings with benefits, have about €130 less in disposable income per month on average.
Labore supplemented its simulation with register and statistical data. These showed declines in both the share of employees receiving housing and unemployment benefits and the average sums paid between February 2024 and February 2025.
Part-time employees recorded larger losses. Average reductions in benefits were, in most cases, about twice as large for part-time employees as for full-time workers.
The position of unemployed people also weakened during the period covered by the study. Average unemployment benefits fell between March 2024 and January 2026.
The share of unemployment benefit recipients receiving earnings-related unemployment allowance fell from about 40 per cent at the start of 2024 to 33 per cent in January 2026.
The poverty rate among unemployed people rose from 49.4 per cent in 2023 to about 56 per cent in 2025, according to the study.
Labore also found a change in the distribution of disposable income. The lowest-income five per cent have nearly €1,000 less a year on average under the April 2026 system than they would have received under the 2023 rules. The highest-income five per cent have gained more than €2,000 a year.
The changes have increased Finland’s Gini coefficient, a measure of income inequality, by 0.84 points to 29.42, roughly the same as the EU average for 2024. The number of children living in low-income households has increased by almost 26,000 compared with the result produced by the previous tax-benefit system.
Green League chair Sofia Virta said the figures reflected decisions taken by the government rather than an unintended development.
“Finland has traditionally been a model country for small income differences,” Virta said in a party statement. She said government policy had moved Finland towards the European average for income inequality during one parliamentary term.
Virta also criticised reductions in unemployment security, housing support and other benefits alongside tax reductions benefiting higher earners. Her comments represent the Green League’s interpretation of the Labore findings.
Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela also cited the report in criticism of the government. She said reductions in social security had affected both benefit recipients and people in employment.
“The cuts have also increased poverty among working people,” Koskela said in a party statement.

J&K may bring electric 'dog sticks' under arms rules as authorities flag animal cruelty concerns and warn against their use on street dogs
SRINAGAR: Electronically operated, shock-delivering “dog sticks” advertised online as protection against street dogs may be brought under the ambit of J&K Arms Rules, 2016, the govt has announced as such devices come under scrutiny for alleged violations of laws against animal cruelty.In a statement issued late Saturday, J&K’s housing and urban development department (HUDD) cautioned that electric shock guns, stun devices, electric prods or similar devices should not be used for stray animals as they inflict unnecessary pain on them and contravene Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960.The advisory has been triggered by the online ads about such “dog sticks” from “M/s Gambs Enterprises”, a Pulwama private firm. The department said it was examining the legal classification of such devices, the authority under which they are sold and their intended use.“All dog catchers, agencies, contractors, animal welfare organisations, municipal bodies and the public are advised not to procure or use electric shock devices for catching, restraining or handling street dogs,” the statement reads. CM Omar Abdullah handles the department.
HUDD secretary Mandeep Kour was not available for comment.The statement says specific licences are required under Section 5 of Arms Rules for sale, transfer or possession of “prescribed classes of arms”, adding not having such documents amount to violations.
“The Arms Rules, 2016 specifically regulate Electronic Disabling Devices (EDDs). Depending upon their statutory classification and specifications, such devices may fall within the restricted or permissible arms categories, and Rule 89(3) provides that EDDs shall be sold only through authorised arms and ammunition dealers holding the requisite licence,” the statement says.J&K recorded over 2 lakh dog-bite cases in the past two years -- 1.2 lakh in Jammu and around 80,000 in the Valley. In Jammu district alone, 33,065 cases were reported in 2024 and 43,759 in 2025, taking its two-year total to 76,824. Srinagar had 12,557 cases in 2024 and 12,592 in 2025. A Srinagar municipal corporation survey in 2023 estimated the number of stray dogs at 64,416.

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Venezuela is expected to face two new tropical waves this week after heavy rains caused flooding and river overflows in Caracas and surrounding areas.
The National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMEH) said tropical wave 41 is currently over northeastern French Guiana and is expected to reach Venezuela between Monday and Tuesday.
Tropical wave 42 is moving across the central tropical Atlantic and could reach Venezuela’s Essequibo region between Thursday and Friday.
INAMEH forecast rainfall and thunderstorms of varying intensity across much of the country on Sunday.
Heavier rainfall is expected in several regions, including Bolivar and Amazonas in southern Venezuela; Anzoategui and Monagas in the east; Lara and Zulia in the west and northwest; and the Andes in western Venezuela.
The forecast follows heavy rains on Saturday that caused flooding and river overflows in Caracas and Miranda state.
More than 60 vehicles were affected after the Guaire River overflowed onto the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas, according to local media reports.
Flooding was also reported in the Coche and La Vega areas, while the Guaire River rose significantly in Petare.
In Miranda state, a house collapsed in the Los Cerritos sector of Los Teques, while authorities reported people missing after vehicles were swept away by rising waters.
Venezuelan authorities activated the Civil Protection System following the heavy rains associated with tropical wave 40.
Response teams were deployed in several areas of Greater Caracas and Miranda state, according to the Venezuelan News Agency.
Acting President Delcy Rodriguez ordered the activation of emergency mechanisms and said authorities were monitoring weather conditions and vulnerable areas. Authorities have urged residents in areas affected by heavy rainfall to remain alert.

The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:55:44 UTC
03:55:44 KST

The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration
Lauren Edwards’ campaign is trying to restart a stalled process to legalized assisted dying in England and Wales — and she’s taking cues from her native Australia.
People gather outside the U.K. Parliament in London during the House of Lords' second reading of the assisted dying bill, on Sept. 12, 2025. | Peter Nicholls/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain is still lagging behind Australia when it comes to assisted dying. But one Labour MP who has seen the debate in both countries is hoping she can push forward a thwarted attempt at change in the U.K.
“If I had six months to live and I was facing a potentially very frightening, very painful, very uncomfortable death, I would want to be able to have the choice to choose to end my life surrounded by my family,” Lauren Edwards, who became an MP in 2024 — and hails from Melbourne, Australia, tells POLITICO in an interview.
Edwards’ support for assisted dying is shaped in part by the laws in Victoria, where she still has family. In 2017, it became the first Australian state to legalize assisted dying for people expected to die within six months, or 12 months for those with neurodegenerative diseases, and who face unacceptable suffering.
Advertisement
Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue.
It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand.
Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around.
It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live.
“When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.”
Sense-checking the legislation with family down under was “really important” when weighing up whether to support Leadbeater’s earlier proposals, she says.
Edwards has Australian friends who have settled in Britain too — and contrasts a friend able to attend his mother’s assisted death in Australia with British families currently worried about prosecution for helping relatives to die. U.K. law punishes the offense with up to 14 years in prison.
Lauren Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model. | House of Commons
“[The] status quo is not neutral. It is not benign,” Edwards argues. “It is a situation where, if we don’t make this legislative change, unfortunately, we will be allowing that pain, fear and isolation.”
In October 2024, an independent review of assisted dying in Victoria by the state Department of Health’s Centre for Evaluation and Research Evidence found the system to be safe and “operating as intended” with “no reports of ineligible individuals” accessing substances to end their lives.
However, access to assisted dying varies across the vast state — which is only slightly smaller than the entire U.K. — and just “a few practitioners” deliver the majority of care. Victoria has been urged to press the central Australian government for more funding.
Advertisement
Choice of priorities
Back in the U.K., the main political parties have agreed that the decision to legalize assisted dying should be a matter for parliament, rather than any one administration. MPs were not whipped to vote in any particular way on Leadbeater’s bill, and the issue is treated as a matter of conscience.
But there was tacit endorsement for the most recent attempted overhaul from the top of Keir Starmer’s government. Before entering No. 10, Starmer promised broadcaster Esther Rantzen — who has stage four lung cancer — that he’d make time for a vote in parliament.
Leadbeater’s bill also received technical support from civil servants in the Department for Health and Social Care and the Ministry of Justice to ensure its workability.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham appears to have other ideas. Burnham was not an MP when assisted dying passed the Commons last year and abstained in a 2015 vote during a previous stint in parliament.
More strikingly, when asked about his stance on the issue last month, Burnham said “the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care” needs to happen first — and argued it would be “very challenging” to introduce assisted dying without substantial progress on these two running policy sores.
Edwards remains bullish. She commends the PM’s commitment to sustainably funding social care — Burnham has kicked off cross-party talks on the issue and asked for a speedier inquiry — and she insists his professed skepticism hasn’t put her off.
Advertisement
“It’s really important that we consider them together,” Edwards says of social care and assisted dying. “I don’t think that there is a reason to delay” changing the law, she argues, highlighting £125 million provided by Starmer’s government for adult and children’s hospices. (A Public Accounts Committee report said this one-off funding did not directly pay for service delivery or solve financial problems facing the sector.)
Edwards’ bill has a four-year implementation period. That means if it becomes law next year, assisted dying wouldn’t be permitted until 2031. She believes the two systems can work on a “dual track” and that poor palliative care won’t incentivize people to access assisted dying.
“I don’t necessarily think that lack of care is a motivator for this option,” she argues. “I think it’s a last resort when physical suffering really can’t be relieved.”
Yvette Cooper speaks during a visit to a care home in London on July 29, 2026. | Pool photo by Kirsty Wigglesworth via WPA/Getty Images
From MPs to peers
A majority of Starmer’s Cabinet backed the bill last time, including Health Secretary Yvette Cooper and Justice Secretary Alex Norris — but only 12 MPs need to switch sides for the bill to fall, making the margins tight. Indeed, suspended Labour MP Karl Turner told POLITICO he’ll vote against the bill after abstaining last June.
“People’s views are largely what I expect them to be when we next vote on this,” Edwards argues. “We haven’t seen any significant moves away from people who were supportive of the bill.”
Then there is the substantive question of the House of Lords. Edwards condemns the “small minority” of peers she blames for filibustering the previous bill. She said she is happy to work with peers on good faith amendments in the “scrutiny process” this time around.
Advertisement
The pro-assisted dying camp will be relying on a little-used pair of laws — the Parliament Acts — which would, in narrow circumstances, allow a bill to be passed despite being deadlocked or defeated by peers in the House of Lords again. “I want to get it back to [peers] ASAP so that they will have the maximum amount of time to finish the job of scrutinizing,” Edwards says.
An impassioned opposition campaign last time around argued Leadbeater’s bill was not safe. The Royal College of Psychiatrists, while neutral on the principle of assisted dying, said it could not support her plans due to a lack of clarity about their profession’s role in the process and whether adequate resources are in place.
While Edwards may struggle to win over Burnham, she hopes to “sit down and have a conversation” with the prime minister before MPs return from recess in September.
One open question remains: how Starmer himself will vote. As prime minister, he voted for it, but didn’t explain his reasoning. Now freed from the constraints of government, Edwards hopes Starmer will make an intervention.
“He has a well-known legal background, is very considered and is obviously a really crucial voice,” she says. Starmer’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Alonzo Carter goes dancing to the big time as Sacramento State makes the transition to the FBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:53:01 UTC
03:53:01 KST

Alonzo Carter goes dancing to the big time as Sacramento State makes the transition to the FBS
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — When the news came in February that Sacramento State’s elevation to the highest level of college football would come a year earlier than expected with an invitation to the Mid-American Conference, coach Alonzo Carter broke out his old dance moves and performed the “Return of the Mack” for his players.
Then it was time to get to work as Carter had been on the job for only about two months and his one-year runway for the transition from being a Championship Subdivision team to an Bowl Subdivision team was gone.
“It was post signing day, post portal period closing so it was a little surprise,” he said. “We knew there was a possibility, but we figured we’d have a year to build it. But once it sunk in and it was going to be ‘26, I went back to my players and told them, ’Hey man, we’re playing this now.’”
From MC Hammer dancer to football coach
Luckily for Carter, both dancing and coaching football are second nature for him. The former backup dancer and choreographer for legendary rap star MC Hammer has spent more than three decades as a football coach, going from a head coach at the high school and junior college level near his hometown of Oakland to an assistant at both San Jose State and Arizona.
Carter said lessons he learned as a young man on tour have carried over to his coaching career and he looks forward to having the rap star come to a few games this season.
“I’m very thankful for having MC Hammer in my life,” he said. “A lot of people go how do you go from dancing to coaching? Well, he gave me a lot of responsibility then. He put me in a leadership position, leadership role. Just watching his work ethic, seeing how he moved day to day becoming one of the all time best in the history of hip hop.”
Hornets look to build on recent success
Athletic director Mark Orr said that Carter is a much better football coach than dancer and believes he’s the right man to shepherd the Hornets through this challenging transition.
Sacramento State won three Big Sky Conference titles and made the playoffs four times in a five-year span from 2019-23. The Hornets went 7-5 last season in the first year under Brennan Marion, who left for the offensive coordinator job at Colorado.
Now Carter takes over a team with just a handful of returning starters and 72 newcomers on the roster, including quarterback Carson Conklin, who returns after spending last season as a backup at Fresno State. The Hornets have about $7 million from the school in NIL funding and a stadium that will hold about 22,000 fans with hopes of building a new stadium soon.
The move to FBS is part of a larger strategy to raise the profile of the athletic department at Sacramento State in hopes that it will do the same for the entire university. Enrollment is up to about 32,000 students and has increased nearly 7% since 2014.
“Athletics, particularly college football, is a front porch and a gateway for prospective students and for alumni to get engaged with their university,” Orr said. “We see it in our admissions applications. We see it on our alumni engagement. We see in our community partnerships. So it’s really important.”
The decision to join the MAC
Orr hired former NBA star Mike Bibby as men’s basketball coach before last season and now the Hornets are headed to the FBS level for football. Playing football in the MAC will require four long road trips to the Midwest, starting with the opener at Eastern Michigan on Saturday. The other Hornets programs will stay local after joining the Big West, with 10 schools in California plus Utah Valley.
“There are a select number of universities that are able to play FBS football. It’s not a sign up,” Orr said. “You have to be invited to play FBS football. There’s 10 FBS conferences in the country and the Mid-American Conference fits, while it may not fit geographically, it fits a lot of the mission and ideals we have as a university and as athletic programs.”
The move up a level gives the Hornets a chance to play two midweek “MACtion” games in November on an ESPN channel, along with three other nationally televised games, including a home matchup against fellow first-year FBS team North Dakota State on the main ESPN channel Sept. 19.
They also will be bowl eligible immediately following an NCAA rule change with a chance to make their first bowl game since losing the Pasadena Bowl to Grambling State in 1968. It also means that a terrific season could put the program in the mix for a College Football Playoff berth and some big-time exposure and money.
There also is another benefit that is particularly exciting for the players — being part of the EA Sports video game.
“That’s a dream for me,” running back Jamar Curtis said. “Honestly, I’ve never been in a video game my whole life. I’m excited. I got little nephews and stuff, little cousins, they use me. So I feel like that’s exciting.”
The excitement goes beyond the players, with linebacker Derek Houston saying he has noticed a different buzz around campus since the move up. Now the key is capitalizing on that to build a team that can contend in the MAC.
“Not everyone really knows what the FCS is,” he said. “They don’t think it’s really D-I, so when you get the FBS label, people get really excited about it.”

49ers take star TE George Kittle off PUP list 10 days before leaving for Australia
SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — San Francisco 49ers star tight end George Kittle was taken off the physically unable to perform list on Sunday, providing hope that he might be able to return from a ruptured right Achilles tendon before the season opener.
The 49ers got good news on the injury front 10 days before the team was set to depart for Australia for a Week 1 game against the Los Angeles Rams on Sept. 11 with both Kittle and All-Pro running back Christian McCaffrey both back at practice.
The Niners are scheduled to leave for Australia on Sept. 2 and Kittle said last week that he needed to get practice time in pads before then to determine whether he would make the trip and try to play Week 1.
Kittle ruptured his Achilles on Jan. 11 in a playoff win at Philadelphia and has made an impressive recovery to get back on the field in less than eight months.
Kittle is a two-time All-Pro and seven-time Pro Bowler who is a key part of San Francisco’s offense as a passing threat and a blocker in the run game. He had 57 catches for 628 yards receiving and seven touchdowns last season.
McCaffrey had missed the past two weeks of practice with what the team had described as “tightness.” After being limited to four games because of injuries in 2024, McCaffrey was an ironman last season. He played 1,010 offensive snaps in the regular season and playoffs — just the ninth running back in the past 20 seasons to top the 1,000 mark — and became the second player in the past decade with at least 450 combined carries and catches.
The 30-year-old McCaffrey hasn’t responded well in the past following his heaviest-use seasons. The previous two times he topped 400 touches — in 2019 with Carolina and 2023 with the 49ers — he was severely hampered by injuries the following season, missing 13 games each in 2020 and 2024.
Star defensive end Nick Bosa remains out of practice with soreness and tendinitis in his surgically repaired right knee. Bosa tore his right ACL in Week 3 last season. He started camp on the active roster but has only participated in individual drills before being shut down nearly three weeks ago. The Niners have expressed optimism that he will be ready for Week 1.

Albanese to override Queensland to settle AI data centre energy rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:53:00 UTC
03:53:00 KST

Albanese to settle AI data centre energy rules, overriding defiant Queensland
In short:
The federal government expects to settle new rules for how data centres use energy in Australia at Wednesday's national cabinet, despite Queensland confirming it will remain opposed to the plan.
Queensland's rejection of rules tying data centre construction to new renewables projects means the federal government will be forced to legislate to override the state.
What's next?
National cabinet will meet on Wednesday, where leaders will also discuss the gun buyback scheme and the next stage of a national plan on family violence.
The federal government expects to settle new energy and water rules for massive AI data centres at a national cabinet meeting on Wednesday despite Queensland's opposition, forcing it to create laws that override the defiant state.
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has sworn to stand his ground at Wednesday's meeting against rules that would require data centre projects to purchase their power from new renewable energy projects, backed by gas, so the energy-hungry facilities do not create more demand that would push up power prices.
The Queensland and Northern Territory governments say they will not sign on to a standard that ties data centres to renewable projects at the exclusion of coal and gas.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen had already flagged the federal government's intention to legislate so-called "causer pays" energy rules next year for big facilities, even if all states and territories signed on, allowing the Commonwealth to overrule dissenters and prevent data centre proponents from playing the states off against each other.
On Sunday, Mr Bowen said the government would find agreement with the states if it could, and legislate to ride over the top of those who opposed the federal government.
"The Queensland government's made their views pretty clear; we disagree with them, and we're proceeding without them," Mr Bowen said.
"Queensland wants to take an open slather approach, let data centres be data centres approach. We don't agree with that.
"We want data centre investment in Australia, but we want it to be in the best interest of Australians, and we're not going to let Queensland run a race to the bottom which would see energy bills go up and reliability go down because they want data centres at any cost."
The federal Coalition is questioning how the Albanese government intends to grant itself powers to override Queensland's energy rules, saying that doing so could be unconstitutional.
"How is Chris Bowen going to nationalise this? What powers is he going to use? The fact now he is going to use desperate measures and probably unconstitutional measures to try and force Queensland and the Northern Territory to take a particular course of action is just absurd," Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said.
"He hasn't been clear on what he wants to use. It looks like he is going to attempt to use the Corporations [Act] power, which would bring with it all types of legal uncertainty."
Queensland to require community buy-in
The Queensland government says energy sources for data centres should remain technology-agnostic.
In a statement, Mr Crisafulli said his government would develop its own framework that ensured communities and local councils also had a say in data centre proposals.
Under Queensland's proposal, data centres would be required to provide a social impact assessment and a community benefit agreement with the relevant local council before lodging a development application, similar to reforms to how battery storage and solar farm projects are assessed in that state.
Mr Crisafulli said data centre deals must be done with the backing of councils and communities.
"This is about data sovereignty for our country, it's about respecting communities' wishes and resources, and it's about creating the jobs of tomorrow while protecting the Queensland of today," Mr Crisafulli said.
The federal government wants data centres to bring their own energy supply to shield against a US-style populist backlash to such facilities.
Community resistance has mired construction in the US, where facilities have strained local electricity grids and caused anxiety in water-scarce communities.
Dozens of US data centre projects worth more than $US100 billion ($140 billion) have been blocked or delayed by local opposition this year, according to US group Data Center Watch.
Settling minimum standards for data centres would also provide investors more certainty on what to expect when dealing with Australia.
While data centre energy demands are expected to triple in the next four years, the government estimates investment plans announced over the past three years alone could be worth more than $100 billion to the Australian economy.
Tying data centres to renewables would fuel backlash: Coalition
The federal government also hopes the new rules will help get more renewables projects over the line.
Many are struggling to reach a final investment decision despite the government underwriting them through the Capacity Investment Scheme, due to a lack of energy buyers willing to strike a Power Purchase Agreement that would guarantee demand for the projects.
At least nine of the renewables projects announced under the Capacity Investment Scheme have since withdrawn, and most projects that have won underwriting support are yet to reach a final investment decision.
Mr Tehan said the government was putting social licence for data centres in jeopardy by tying them to renewables.
"This policy on AI and data centres shouldn't be trying to make up for Chris Bowen's abject failures. The fact that he can't get renewable energy projects up shouldn't be an excuse for tying states and territories to this policy," he said.
"They're saying there needs to be social licence around data centres, but they're also saying, 'We're not worried about there being no social licence when it comes to renewable energy.' If you tie the two hand-in-glove together, it's going to lead to an even bigger backlash."
While the Coalition is at odds with government over its move to force data centres to run on renewables, the major parties are working to find common ground on a longer-term AI policy and the massive economic potential offered by artificial intelligence.
Last week, the major parties agreed to establish a dedicated committee to inquire into AI issues in the hopes of progressing some of those policy questions.
Mr Tehan said the Coalition wanted to work with the government on AI where it was in the national interest.
"We've shown that over the last fortnight when it came to reform of the NDIS, reform of media bargaining codes, so we will continue where it is in the national interest," he said.
"And given the importance of this sector going forward and making sure that it's established here in Australia in a way that works for everyone, especially those in regional and rural Australia, I think it is critically important, and we can work with government to achieve that."

Halis Sünnetci
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Dominik Szoboszlai converted a penalty in the ninth minute of stoppage time as Liverpool came from behind twice to earn a dramatic 2-2 draw against Newcastle United on Sunday.
Anthony Elanga gave Newcastle an early lead at St. James’ Park before Cody Gakpo equalized in the second half.
Substitute Joe Willock restored the hosts’ advantage less than three minutes later, but Szoboszlai’s late spot kick denied Newcastle victory in Matthias Jaissle’s first Premier League match in charge.
Newcastle opened the scoring through a counterattack in the fifth minute.
Liverpool left space in midfield, allowing William Osula to surge forward before playing Elanga through on goal. The Swedish winger finished calmly past Alisson Becker and into the bottom-left corner.
The goal ended Elanga’s run of 40 league appearances without scoring, dating back to April 2025.
Liverpool nearly equalized in the 18th minute. Rio Ngumoha’s cross was overhit, but the visitors regained possession and Milos Kerkez delivered another ball into the area.

Newcastle threatened again in the 24th minute when Yoane Wissa played Osula into the area. Jeremy Jacquet applied pressure, while Alisson left his line quickly to smother the forward’s attempt.
The hosts maintained their advantage until halftime despite Liverpool controlling more possession and winning several corners.
Liverpool drew level in the 54th minute through Gakpo.
Ryan Gravenberch played a direct pass to his fellow Dutchman, who turned and advanced toward the penalty area before drilling a powerful shot into the bottom-left corner.
Newcastle responded almost immediately.
Wissa led a counterattack and released Joe Willock, who had entered the match moments earlier. The midfielder cut inside and curled a shot past Alisson from about 20 yards, with the ball striking the post before crossing the line in the 57th minute.
Wissa came close to extending Newcastle’s lead in the 68th minute but failed to connect with Lewis Hall’s low cross across the six-yard box.
Alisson then kept Liverpool in the match in the 86th minute, racing off his line and blocking Wissa’s low effort with his legs.
Liverpool were awarded a penalty deep into stoppage time after substitute Victor Munoz drove into the area and was brought down by Hall.
Szoboszlai stepped up and powered the penalty into the top-left corner in the 99th minute, giving Hornicek no chance.
The result gave Newcastle and Liverpool one point each from their opening match of the Premier League season.

Zaidi received a written message from Libyan National Unity Government’s Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh emphasizing “the importance of consolidating and strengthening bilateral relations between Iraq and Libya,” according to a statement from his office.
The message also included an official invitation for the Iraqi prime minister to visit Libya “at the earliest possible opportunity” and stressed the importance of continued coordination and consultations to align positions at international forums regarding challenges facing the Arab region.
Zaidi said Iraq was “determined to build the best possible foreign relations with brothers and friends.”
He emphasized the importance Baghdad attaches to opportunities for cooperation and economic integration to “strengthen capabilities, support sustainable development and reinforce the foundations of a positive partnership.”
Baour arrived in Baghdad earlier Sunday for an official visit of an unspecified duration to participate in meetings of the Libyan-Iraqi Joint Committee on Sunday and Monday, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The committee is reconvening after a 25-year hiatus.
Upon his arrival, Baour held talks with Hussein on bilateral relations and ways to develop cooperation in various fields.
They also discussed regional and international issues of mutual concern and exchanged views on them, the ministry said.
The Libyan-Iraqi Joint Committee is a high-level institutional framework intended to strengthen bilateral relations and facilitate agreements covering economy, trade, investment, health, education and security.
The precise date of the committee’s establishment could not be confirmed, but sources told Anadolu that its first session was held in 2000, when the two countries agreed that it would convene annually.
Its second and most recent session was held in the Libyan capital Tripoli in 2001.
The committee’s meetings were subsequently suspended following the 2003 US invasion of Iraq and the fall of Saddam Hussein’s government, followed by the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s government in Libya in 2011.

Russian volunteers shoot down much-hyped Ukrainian missile with machine-gun (VIDEO)
A small Russian mobile air defense unit consisting of volunteers has successfully shot down a Ukrainian missile Kiev touted as its “most successful” weapon by firing at it with a machine gun, according to Kursk Region Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein.
The intercept occurred during a Ukrainian drone and missile attack overnight on Sunday. According to Khinshtein, the BARS-Kursk brigade, made up predominantly of residents of the border region, received an alert about an incoming strike. “Minutes later,” one of its mobile air defense units detected a “huge” missile traveling at 500 kilometers per hour at an altitude of less than 50 meters. The soldiers managed to hit the missile, forcing it to lose altitude and eventually fall into a wooded area.
A video of the intercept recorded by BARS-Kursk soldiers and published by Khinshtein shows the unit detecting the projectile flying at a low altitude and shooting at it. The missile is then shown crashing into the ground in a massive fiery blast. The second part of the video shows soldiers examining the wreckage at the crash site.
The Russian military was able to retrieve the missile’s mission input data from the wreckage and determine that the projectile, with a range of 3,000 kilometers and carrying a warhead with explosives equivalent to a ton of TNT, was aimed at a “strategic facility” in Tula Region in central Russia.
“Our volunteers did not just shoot down a missile. They prevented a catastrophe and saved human lives,” the governor said, vowing to recommend the air defense unit servicemen for a decoration. He also called it an example “of what a Russian solider is capable of.”
The Ukrainian military has been routinely targeting civilian and energy infrastructure in their drone and missile strikes deep into Russian territory. Moscow has condemned the Ukrainian strikes on Russia’s civilian infrastructure and residential areas as terrorist attacks, adding that they are apparently intended to compensate for Kiev’s setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces continue their steady advance.
Russia has been responding to those attacks by intensifying long-range missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.
Unveiled in 2025, the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile has been repeatedly touted by Kiev as a state-of-the-art weapon. Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky described it last year as “by far the most successful missile in Ukraine’s arsenal.” The missile is produced by Fire Point – a Ukrainian defense contractor personally promoted by Zelensky during his trips to Western nations.
The company was later revealed to be de facto owned by the Ukrainian leader’s longtime former business partner Timur Mindich, known as “Zelensky’s wallet” in Kiev. The businessman fled Ukraine last year after a major corruption scandal in which he was named as one of the primary suspects.

Tusk’s stance on Nord Stream motivated by ‘economic expediency’ – Putin
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s position on the Nord Stream pipeline sabotage is motivated by the fact that Warsaw lost out economically on the project, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in an interview with Vesti published on Sunday.
The statement came just days after Tusk said that those responsible for the September 2022 blasts should not be ashamed, but rather those who built the pipelines. Warsaw had long opposed the pipelines’ construction over concerns about Europe’s dependence on Russian energy, he told reporters on Thursday.
According to Putin, the Polish prime minister’s “motives are very simple – economic expediency.”
The initial plan for the Nord Stream project envisioned one of the pipelines going through Poland, he said. However, the decision was ultimately made to “to run the second line along the bottom of the Baltic Sea in order to minimize risks,” he added.
Even back then, Warsaw was against this, Putin added.
“Partly because it would lose certain economic advantages for Poland as a transit country. Secondly, Poland would lose revenue from the transit of our hydrocarbons. This position is absolutely nothing new,” he said.
Tusk’s statement came a day after a Ukrainian national suspected of taking part in the bombing of the Nord Stream pipelines was arrested in Croatia on a European warrant.
German investigators maintain that the sabotage was carried out by a small group of Ukrainians who used counterfeit documents to rent a sailing yacht and transport military-grade explosives to waters off the Danish island of Bornholm. There, the group allegedly used commercial diving equipment to set the charges on the pipelines at a depth of around 100 meters.
Moscow has long dismissed the theory as fantasy, arguing that the operation could not have been carried out in NATO-controlled waters without state backing.
In a 2024 interview with American journalist Tucker Carlson, Putin hinted that the blasts were likely orchestrated by the CIA.
