After 10 years at United, CEO Scott Kirby is thinking big about the future of his airline from JFK to AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

NEWARK, New Jersey — Scott Kirby says he doesn't believe in revenge.
"Everyone thinks I do, but no, I don't," said the United Airlines CEO, whom American Airlines fired 10 years ago, when he was president of that carrier. "I compete aggressively."
United announced it had hired him as president on Aug. 29, 2016, a blink after American disclosed his departure. Now, Kirby is running the second-most profitable U.S. airline after Delta Air Lines. And his former employer, American, is a distant third of the big, more-than-century-old, U.S. carriers, though it's working to ramp up revenue through a host of upgrades, including bringing back seatback screens.
Kirby floated the idea of megamergers with both Delta and American in the past year, combinations that would bring together some of the biggest airlines in the world. He's so far been rebuffed, and antitrust experts were skeptical about the possibility.
He's thinking bigger than he has before as the industry faces ever-higher costs, limited airport infrastructure and a population that's ready to shell out more to fly — often in the expensive seats — to the next "it" destination.
Eyeing JFK from EWR
CNBC rode with Kirby from the west side of Midtown Manhattan to United's hub at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey earlier this month, where the 59-year-old executive outlined his vision for the carrier before his flight.
Kirby said he wants to expand United's footprint at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport after his airline returns to the congested airport through a partnership with American's former partner, JetBlue Airways, as early as next year.
"We got a bunch of irons in the fire to try to find ways to do it," he said, adding that United could at some point acquire slots from carriers that aren't flying profitable routes out of the airport.
And while United already holds the crown among U.S. airlines for international flights, which are in high demand among U.S. tourists, he wants to expand the carrier's footprint abroad even more. This week, United is set to announce a host of new international routes, the carrier's annual splash that has previously included new dots on the map like Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia and Bilbao, Spain.
United has been touting its international expansion for years, saying its vast network acts as a driver for customer loyalty and sign-ups for lucrative travel rewards credit cards. Its route announcements typically come with much fanfare.
Kirby, a three-decade airline executive, is the United States' most outspoken airline CEO. His team knows this, and they've stopped telling him well in advance what will be on tap for the next batch of Instagram-friendly routes.
"They no longer tell me in advance because they're afraid I'll spill the beans, which is fair," he said.
While Delta has still had a lead on profits, CEO Ed Bastian doesn't want to give up ground to United. It is starting to expand flights over the Pacific, a United stronghold.
"People say, 'Well, when is it someone else's turn?' Well, I'm never going to let that be someone else's turn. It's always our turn," Bastian told students at Columbia Business School in April 2024. "We always get a chance to prove it every single day. ... Yesterday really doesn't matter. It's only today and tomorrow that you can think about."
1 minute break
It's been a decade since Kirby started at United. He joined the airline in August 2016 after he was let go by American when he was president and didn't have a path to eventually becoming CEO.
United dropped a securities filing just after American disclosed Kirby's departure, saying he would be taking the president role at the Chicago airline. American promoted then-Chief Operating Officer Robert Isom to president that day, Kirby's old role. Isom was named American's next CEO in late 2021.
"I joke that most people take a few weeks, a couple months between jobs. I took 60 seconds," Kirby said.
United promoted Kirby to CEO from president in May 2020, while the industry was reeling from Covid, its worst-ever crisis.
The executive ranks at the tops of United and American trace their roots back to America West and other airlines, before a wave of mergers over the past two decades left four carriers holding more than three-quarters of U.S. flight capacity.
"One of the things also I learned at American: There's only so much change you can make as the No. 2," he said. "You can push too hard and you get fired."
United was in the midst of upgrading its cabins when Kirby joined in 2016, including with its highest-end Polaris pod seats for long-haul business class. But he said his first order of business was going through money-losing routes with a highlighter to figure out what was working and what wasn't.
The company considered closing its bases at Los Angeles International Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport in Virginia. Kirby said he stopped that idea, and both stayed open.
The airports are critical for United. LAX is one of the airline's most important hubs, though no carrier has a handle on that airport like they do others. And Kirby took a day trip from his son's soccer camp in Brazil last month to fly up to meet with President Donald Trump to unveil a $22.5 billion revamp of Dulles in the Oval Office.
AI, mergers and the future of travel
Stock analysts and legal experts were highly skeptical about a merger between United and one of the other U.S. giants.
People familiar with the matter said Kirby approached Delta but was turned down, as The Wall Street Journal first reported last month. The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the talks. Delta declined to comment. The carrier's president, Peter Carter, told CNBC at an industry conference in June that he doesn't see a merger or acquisition in Delta's future.
American, meanwhile, publicly rejected a merger offer from United this spring.
"At the end of the day, we spend time looking at things that have a chance of happening. We don't spend a lot of time pursuing impossibilities," Isom told CNBC in an interview in late June.
Kirby told CNBC that he hasn't changed his stance and he's not interested in acquiring a smaller airline, like JetBlue. "That's still the case," he said.
"Everything I say would require a willing partner," Kirby said.
When asked about antitrust concerns and likely pushback from state attorneys general, he said, "All of the objections are ... based on a premise that the airline industry is a commodity."
And Kirby said the industry has since evolved and that Delta and United have differentiated themselves, with their routes, onboard cabins and other products.
He said he wants United to grow in South America and in the Southeast U.S., but there's a lack of places to build out new hubs that make sense.
"Those are two places that are holes for United that are hard to fix on a stand-alone basis," Kirby said.
The best place for serving South America is Miami International Airport, he added. American had a more than 60% share of passenger enplanements in the 2025 fiscal year, according to airport data.
Putting mergers aside, Kirby said artificial intelligence tools for both employees and customers will make traveling easier and improve reliability, a tall order for any airline that is susceptible to weather, constrained airports and a host of other daily surprises from mechanical problems.
He wants delays expressed in clear English to customers.
"I firmly believe in no excuses, and so we don't make excuses," he said.
Even still, in the first half of the year, United ranked behind Delta and Alaska Airlines, which recently merged with Hawaiian Airlines, for on-time arrivals, according to the Transportation Department.
Kirby said outside factors or outright crises will always challenge the industry and said he is focused on the long-term future of the airline.
"Our employees often ask me like, 'What keeps you awake at night,' and I tell them, 'nothing,'" he said. "My job is to set the company up so none of you ever have to have a sleepless night worrying about your jobs."
He said his goal is to never have another furlough at the airline.
When asked if he would retire eventually, Kirby said, "I hope I will know when to retire and do it gracefully with a great transition with great people."

United's next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

In August 2018, the then-president and now CEO of United Airlines Scott Kirby told a room of reporters at an aviation conference in Denver about the airline's big plans for the new Boeing 737 Max 10: lie-flat, premium seats and a host of profitable, transcontinental routes.
The plane was supposed to start flying in 2020.
Hundreds of those seats have been in storage because its certification — which was expected more than six years ago — is far behind schedule. Now, Boeing and many of its customers expect the company to win federal approval for the plane, the largest in the bestselling 737 Max family, soon, so United has to decide what to do with all those seats.
"We got a bunch of lie-flat seats that we don't know what to do with," Kirby told CNBC during an interview earlier this month at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey. "They don't fit on other airplanes."
United hasn't disclosed the layout it will use on the planes, or where it will fly them. The airline set its earlier plans for the Boeing 737 Max 10 before it even offered a premium economy section.
The delays for both the newly approved Boeing 737 Max 7, the smallest model, and the yet-to-be-certified Max 10 came after the manufacturer had to redesign an anti-icing system. Boeing was also dealing with increased scrutiny after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing won approval for the 737 Max 7 earlier this month, with big customer Southwest Airlines expecting to fly them sometime in the first half of 2027.
United pivoted because of the Boeing delays and recently outfitted a subfleet of its Airbus A321neo narrow-body aircraft with 20 of the newly designed Polaris suites, premium economy options and other new seats as part of the industry's race to add high-yielding seating on its planes. It's dubbed the subfleet the "Coastliner" for transcontinental routes.
But the dimensions and requirements aren't the same on both planes, leaving United with a decision on what its interiors will look like.
It expects to get the first Boeing Max 10s in summer 2027. It has 167 of the aircraft on order, according to its most recent quarterly filing.

Feature: Four decades on, Baidui Cup continues to fuel Beijing's youth football
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:50:16 CST
20:50:16 KST

by sportswriter Li Chunyu
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Returning to the Baidui Cup for the first time as head coach of China's men's national football team, Shao Jiayi found the same passion and desire from young players as he had during his own childhood.
"I competed in the Baidui Cup decades ago, and much of my happiness at that time came from creating exciting moments with my teammates in summer," the 46-year-old said during this year's Baidui Cup, one of Beijing's biggest youth football tournaments.
This year marks the first time that the tournament has two separate groups - recreational and competitive.
The recreational group is open to young football enthusiasts, while the competitive group caters to club youth teams and youth training academies. According to organizers, more than 1,400 teams and over 15,000 players participated in the Baidui Cup this year.
"What touched me most was the fearlessness of the young players," Shao said. "Football demands and encourages physical contact. I saw these kids were willing to go into challenges. Our young talents are really brave and fully enjoy the stage to show themselves."
For Fu Ming, a Chinese referee who returned from FIFA World Cup duty last month, the Baidui Cup is a festival not only for children, but also for referees and officials.
Even with his busy schedule, Fu, 43, has long wanted to officiate the Baidui Cup, viewing it as a valuable opportunity to communicate with young referees and players.
"The World Cup and Baidui Cup differ a lot in intensity, but my attitude towards each game remains the same," Fu said. "My movement and decision-making on the pitch have become second nature. I naturally brought all my habits to the Baidui Cup. Young referees can observe how I position myself and move around the field."
In a competitive U15 match officiated by Fu, referee Chen Xueyang watched on from the sidelines.
"I graduated from Capital University of Physical Education and Sports where Fu instructed me at a football referee training camp," recalled Chen, 25. "After I became a referee, I sometimes sent him video clips of controversial or challenging calls for advice, and he would give me a call right away. He asked for my opinion first and then shared his own perspective."
"Fu gave me tremendous support. He sets an example for our young referees to learn from," Chen added.
Player Niu Yuhao spoke after his team won the match 2-0. "Fu is a world-class referee and controlled the game pace well," he said. "I have been playing football for eight years since primary school. I hope to enjoy football and build up my physical fitness."
After the final whistle, the young players took a group photo with Fu, who also gave many of them his autograph.
"Without joy, there will be no motivation," Fu said. "A football match serves as an excellent lesson for children, through which they can learn to win honorably and accept defeat gracefully. Even though they are opponents on the pitch, they should still help when others are in need."
While the inaugural Baidui Cup in 1984 attracted 112 teams, that number has expanded to over 1,000 in recent years.
"The large number of young football participants in Beijing lays a solid foundation for cultivating more talents in the future. Football fueled by passion will always accompany them on their journey of growth," said Hu Jianping, president of the Beijing Football Association. ■

Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:50:12 UTC
20:50:12 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.
The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time to a demand made by the sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.
“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.
Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.
That shifted when Fedorov, a popular minister who had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.
It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.
Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”
Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.
Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.
“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors in 2027--28.
The US could help by supplying “some small percentage” of its stockpiles – about 5% to 10%, he added. Ukraine was willing to pay and it would mean the country “could get through the winter”, he said, calling on the US to make what would be “a very significant difference both in protecting lives and diplomatically”.
Following a conversation with Zelenskyy on Saturday, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had agreed to strengthen French support for Ukraine, including through the delivery of interceptor missiles, without giving further details.
Ukraine’s allies in the so-called coalition of the willing – an initiative led by France and Britain – will meet on Monday to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.
Russia is seeking to build up forces for a renewed effort to capture the rest of the eastern Donetsk province it does not control by the end of the year, though Zelenskyy said he was confident Moscow would fail to capture the area, comprising principally the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The president said he believed Russia would try to conscript a further 300,000 soldiers after the Russian parliamentary elections in September. It would be a “peripheral mobilisation” conducted away from Moscow, St Petersburg and other main cities in an effort to regain momentum in the almost deadlocked frontline, he said.

Kenya arrests 4 suspects in Amboseli elephant poisoning case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:49:38 CST
20:49:38 KST

NAIROBI, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Four suspects have been arrested following the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem, and authorities are hunting for more suspects, a government official has said.
Rebecca Miano, cabinet secretary in the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife, said in a statement issued on Saturday that 15 of the deaths were recorded between June 24 and July 24, while three more were reported last week.
Miano said the ongoing investigations were yet to establish criminal culpability, adding that the government would allow the investigative and judicial processes to run their course and prosecute anyone found to have unlawfully killed, poisoned or harmed wildlife.
She said the Kenya Wildlife Service, in collaboration with security, investigative and scientific agencies, has intensified its inquiries into the cause of the deaths, noting that comprehensive field investigations, laboratory analysis and environmental sampling have already been undertaken.
According to Miano, preliminary laboratory results point to the probable involvement of a toxic substance, with earlier indications suggesting that cyanide poisoning may have resulted from the ingestion of pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from farms adjacent to wildlife habitats.
However, Miano noted that these findings remain subject to further scientific verification before the investigation is deemed complete.
The official emphasized that the government will enhance monitoring of risks arising from the misuse, illegal application, trafficking or careless handling of hazardous substances that may endanger wildlife, people and ecosystems. ■

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has defended the memorandum of understanding with the U.S. as the best path for the country to move beyond what he described as a state of "neither war nor peace."
In a speech published by state-run IRNA early Sunday, he said members of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council believed the memorandum represented the best possible agreement based on what he described as dignity, wisdom and the national interest.
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
The deal known as the Memorandum of Understanding that U.S. President Donald Trump signed in June set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war with Iran and reaching an accord on its nuclear program.
That period ended last week, but the two sides remain far apart, with no signs of compromise on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global shipping.
Pezeshkian also linked the agreement to Iran’s economic prospects, saying the country could not attract investment in this stalled phase.
“Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk,” he said. “We have to remove this risk from the country.”
Nearly six months into the war with the United States and Israel, the Iranian economy is suffering under sanctions and a naval blockade.
Meanwhile, the hard-line new leader of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council warned Tehran’s neighbors against joining the new U.S. effort to hurt Iran’s economy.
“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Mohsen Rezaei said in an interview with the state broadcaster that aired Saturday.
Rezaei was named this month as part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance. His interview with IRIB is his most extensive public statement since then.
He said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf, alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, if neighbors join what he described as the economic war against Iran.
Trump in the past week has vowed to increase Iran’s pain by imposing an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation. Iran has lived under sanctions for years.
In other developments, Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir will lead an official delegation traveling to Tehran Monday, Iranian state television reported, citing Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei.
Baghaei said the visit aims to strengthen bilateral cooperation between Iran and Pakistan and continue Pakistan’s work to promote peace and security in the region.
Two regional officials said the visit was part Islamabad’s ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States and Iran, and urge both countries to return to the negotiating table. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
The trip announcement came after a phone call between Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. There was no immediate comment from Pakistan, which has led several mediation efforts to end the Iran war.
Munir has made several visits to Iran since Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif assigned him to help defuse tensions between the United States and Iran.

Humanoid robot breaks Usain Bolt's 100m record in China
Humanoid robots smashed sprinting records and competed in boxing, football and martial arts at Beijing’s World Robot Games, including running legend Usain Bolt's record for the 100-metre dash. The robo-athletes drew cheers from hundreds of spectators and showcased China’s growing dominance in humanoid robotics.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Faceless humanoids exceeded human records and delighted hundreds of spectators at the World Robot Games over the weekend in Beijing as China showcased its dominance in the industry.
Dozens of humanoids and their human operators descended on Beijing's Olympic speed skating arena Sunday to compete in events from athletics and boxing to football and martial arts.
During Saturday's opening ceremony, a Chinese robot broke Jamaican legend Usain Bolt's record for the 100-metre dash, a feat splashed across headlines in Chinese state media.
The white and headless humanoid called Tiangong Ultra finished the sprint in 9.39 seconds according to state broadcaster CCTV – surpassing Bolt's best of 9.58 seconds, set in 2009.
On Sunday, robot-makers scored another win, with the same humanoid model shattering the 400-metre world record by nearly five seconds.
Developed by a local government-backed research centre in Beijing, it finished in 38.16 seconds – with its time later revised to 38.15.
In one 400-metre heat, a white-shelled robot thrashed its arms side to side as it propelled itself around the track, leaning dangerously forward as fans wondered out loud if it would fall.
The robot wobbled as it stormed toward the finish but managed to remain upright.
Fans were just as pleased to watch the robo-athletes flop, as multiple robotic runners failed to start.
Others made their way around the track at the pace of a brisk walk or crumbled immediately after the gun start.
Read moreThe era of the machine: Silicon Valley shows off humanoid robots
Children and their parents giggled as a toddler-sized robot kicked a football off the pitch over knee-high barricades.
'It's not a test of intelligence'
Each clunky, barely defended goal earned the waddling humanoids roars of applause from the stands.
Spectators erupted into laughter as a humanoid in a boxing ring stumbled off to the side and folded over the ropes where it stayed motionless until humans lifted it away.
For 72-year-old spectator Hou Yali, the weekend's robot records left her wanting to watch the machines go against humans.
"We'll be able to see more clearly whether machines can surpass humans," said Hou, who is retired and lives in Beijing.
"Right now, this is just running, just a competition of speed. It's not a test of intelligence, or hiring someone to do household tasks or act as live-in help," she said.
Hou, who pays aides to clean her home and make meals for her weekly, said she would like to see robots do those tasks.
"With the development of our country's economy, people have more money in their pockets, and they may decide to use robots," she said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

11:38:04 UTC
20:38:04 KST

Ukrainian drones struck a logistics complex belonging to Russian online retailer Ozon in Orenburg on 23 August, the second Ozon warehouse hit in two days, monitoring Telegram channels reported. The site sits about 1,200 km from the war zone, near Russia's border with Kazakhstan. Hours earlier, a large fire tore through a separate warehouse outside St. Petersburg, roughly 900 km north of Ukraine, though local authorities declared no drone or missile threat.
Drones hit Russia's biggest Ozon warehouse
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published video of the strike moment, after which a fire took hold on the site. Independent Russian outlet Astra analyzed eyewitness footage showing an emergency vehicle racing toward the depot. The complex spans more than 200,000 m² and was designed to hold over 31 million items, ranking among Ozon's biggest in Russia.
The warehouse stands inside the city's special economic zone, a tax-favored industrial park on the eastern edge of European Russia. The first phase opened in August 2024, and a second building followed in 2025.
Orenburg mayor Albert Yumadilov claimed several drones were downed over the special economic zone and that debris fell on the Ozon complex, starting a fire that crews quickly put out with no one hurt.
Ozon confirmed the strike, saying it evacuated more than 300 workers, pulled its goods from the marketplace and stopped taking new deliveries while the site sat idle.
A second fire near St. Petersburg, with no air-raid alert
Overnight, a large blaze hit a warehouse in the Kolpino area south of St. Petersburg. Astra established that the warehouse stood about 350 m from an Ozon site, and witnesses said they heard no drones or air defense. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exile+ identified the burning facility as a storage warehouse run by Logistera.
Part of a widening campaign on Russian marketplace logistics
The Orenburg hit followed the first-ever Ozon strike a day earlier, at a warehouse in Chapaevsk, Samara Oblast. Before turning to Ozon, Ukrainian drones had struck more than 10 warehouses belonging to the larger Russian marketplace Wildberries. Such marketplace hubs move not only consumer goods but dual-use items like electronics and drone components that can reach Russia's military.

Ukraine at 35: Defenseless in the air as Russia advances in Donbass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:36:41 UTC
20:36:41 KST

Ukraine at 35: Defenseless in the air as Russia advances in Donbass
Ukraine is marking the 35th anniversary of its independence, proclaimed on August 24, 1991, amid the disintegration of the Soviet Union. The country meets the anniversary in a bleak state, plagued by an enduring political crisis, a plethora of corruption scandals, the capitulation of its air defenses, and a steadily deteriorating situation on the front line of the conflict with Russia.
In recent weeks, the immediate battlefield situation has been overshadowed by ramped-up long-range strike campaigns waged by both sides of the conflict. Initially touted as an “operation of influence” to force Russia into negotiations on Ukrainian terms, Kiev’s drone attacks have backfired spectacularly. Moscow has retaliated in force, repeatedly striking assorted military industrial sites and dual-use infrastructure, as well as bringing Ukrainian shipping in the Black Sea to a halt. The exchange in strikes has exposed the critical deterioration of Ukrainian air defenses, which are now entirely unable to intercept Russian ballistics.
The front line has been far from static despite longstanding efforts by Ukraine and its Western backers to paint it as a stalemate, and the situation for Kiev has been worsening across multiple key locations.
Here is RT’s look at the latest developments on the front line:
Battle for Slavyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration
Arguably the main events have been unfolding around the Slavyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, a string of cities in the northwest of Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) and the last heavily fortified Ukrainian stronghold in the region. The agglomeration has remained under Kiev’s control for over a decade since the early stage of the conflict in then-Ukrainian Donbass, prompted by the 2014 Maidan coup.
Over the years, the cities were transformed into a single fortified zone by a vast system of reinforced trenches, bunkers, and tunnels. From the east, the agglomeration is additionally protected by the defunct Seversky Donets-Donbass Canal, built in the 1950s to improve the water supply to Donetsk. The canal was shut off by the Ukrainian authorities under the pretext of damage early in the conflict, which heavily strained the water supply to Donetsk, into which Kiev’s militias had fired artillery for years, killing hundreds of civilians.
Following the liberation of Konstantinovka on the southernmost tip of the agglomeration in early July, Russian troops have continued to advance towards Slavyansk-Kramatorsk from multiple directions.
Over the past two weeks, Russian forces have mounted pressure on the town of Druzhkovka, with active combat continuing within the village of Alekseyevo-Druzhkovka, located between Druzhkovka and Konstantinovka. Russian troops appear to have flanked Ukrainian forces from the southwest, with the Defense Ministry in Moscow reporting the liberation of multiple locations in the area, namely the villages of Andreyevka, Nikolaypolye, Novonikolayevka, and Petrovka, over the period.
Moscow’s forces are also apparently seeking to disrupt Ukrainian communications between Slavyansk and Kramatorsk, advancing along a hilly ridge located roughly in between the two cities to the southwest. Over the past two weeks, the Russian military reported seizing the small villages of Orekhovatka and Pershomaryevka, located to the north and south of the ridge, respectively.
Russian forces have also made new gains in the town of Krasny Liman. While technically not a part of the agglomeration, it is located some 20 km to the northeast of Slavyansk across the Seversky Donets River, covering the approach to the stronghold from that direction. The town, which has been heavily damaged during months of intensive combat, is now reportedly largely under Russia’s control.
Zaporozhye offensive
Russia’s Zaporozhye Region has become another major flashpoint lately, with the country’s military actively advancing on the flanks of the town of Orekhov, located around 50 km to the southeast of the regional capital.
Once the staging area for the disastrous 2023 Ukrainian counteroffensive and a major logistics hub, the town ended up on the front line following the liberation of the town of Gulaypole earlier this year. Over the past two weeks, the Russian military has managed to sever a major road approaching the town from the north, liberating the village of Novosoloshino. Russian troops have been expanding the zone of control farther to the north of it into the neighboring Ukrainian region of Dnepropetrovsk, seizing control of the villages of Rybalskoye and Novoye Pole near its border.
Orekhov is now linked to the Ukrainian-controlled city of Zaporozhye only through one major road, which approaches the town from the northwest. Russian forces have reportedly been sighted within less than 1 km of the key artery, the loss of which would leave the Ukrainian garrison supply dependent on dirt roads running across open fields.
Russian forces have also reportedly breached Ukrainian positions between Orekhov and the adjacent village of Malaya Tokmachka, which is believed to have fallen largely under their control. If confirmed, the development effectively means the Russian military has reached the southeastern outskirts of the town itself.
Frontline pressure grows
The continuing advance of Russian troops has not been limited to the two key areas, with Moscow’s forces mounting pressure along the front line. Russian troops have made new gains to the north of Pokrovsk and Mirnograd, two major cities in the southwest of the DPR liberated early this year.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, troops have advanced onto the town of Dobropolye, located some 30 km to the southwest of Druzhkovka, seizing several villages in its vicinity. The active combat in the area has effectively enabled the latest successes around Slavyansk and Kramatorsk, depriving the Ukrainian forces stationed around Dobropolye of maneuver and making them unable to somehow assist the garrison of the agglomeration.
Russian forces have also made new gains in Ukraine’s Kharkov Region, advancing on Ukrainian troops to the southeast of the town of Volchansk. The town has seen intensive hostilities throughout the past year, suffering major ruin in the process. The Russian Defense Ministry announced taking control of the town in late 2025.
The recent advances in the area have put Ukrainian forces stationed to the southeast of the town at risk of encirclement. The remaining troops are now locked between the Volchya River in the north and the Russian focus advancing from the east and west, with the window for their potential retreat rapidly narrowing.

Some 3,000 gather for Swiss cowbell ringing festival
Rhythmic jingling, the clatter of whips or the solemn sounds of the alphorn: since Friday, the town of Schüpfen in canton Bern has been showcasing the full range of sounds and noises that Swiss folklore has to offer.
Over 3,000 active Trychler, Treichler, Trinkler, Trichjer, Scheller, Einscheller, Sonneurs and Schellenders have travelled from all over Switzerland to attend the three-day Swiss National Scheller and Trychler Festival (a gathering to celebrate traditional Swiss cowbell ringing).
Following the ceremonial speeches, at which Swiss minister Albert Rösti is expected to speak, the Trychel groups will set off along two parade routes and send ringing through the tranquil Seeland village of Schüpfen.
+ Is this man the last Swiss cowbell maker?
Bells and cowbells are used as noise-making instruments in many customs across the Alpine region. Often, the aim is to drive away evil spirits or attract good ones with the noise. Numerous noise-making customs take place during the dark winter months. Some are said to have their roots in pre-Christian times.

In Russia, 165 deserted villages were officially liquidated in eight months - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
In 26 regions of Russia, 165 deserted settlements were liquidated in less than eight months of 2026. Villages are disappearing fastest in the Novgorod and Kostroma regions.
The demographic crisis and the extinction of regions in Russia continue to gain momentum. In the first eight months of 2026, 165 deserted settlements were officially liquidated in 26 Russian regions, the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the leaders in the rate of depopulation and legal liquidation of villages were Novgorod Region (according to various estimates, between 21 and 35 villages erased from the map) and Kostroma Region (between 21 and 23 settlements).
At the same time, there are no more empty settlements in Ryazan, Vladimir, Nizhny Novgorod, Novosibirsk and Kemerovo regions, Perm Krai, Karelia and Tatarstan.
Differences in the statistics of local media and independent researchers arise because of bureaucratic delays: regional laws on liquidation are adopted quickly, while changes enter all-Russian registers with a delay. However, the fact remains unchanged - Russia’s hinterland is rapidly emptying out and dying out
As a reminder
In Russia’s regions, police fine people for storing canisters of gasoline and detain them for attempting to complain about unequal access to fuel. Moscow and St. Petersburg have received priority supplies, while gas stations are closing in other regions.

Wartime election would 'destroy' Ukraine, Zelenskiy says

Wartime election would 'destroy' Ukraine, Zelenskiy says
KYIV, Aug 23 - Holding a wartime election in Ukraine while active fighting with Russia continues would "destroy" the country by splitting Ukrainians, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said.
His comments, released to reporters on Sunday, were Zelenskiy's first on the subject since ousted former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a wartime poll in a bombshell address last week.
Fedorov's surprise dismissal last month sparked widespread protests, but supporters calling for his reinstatement later baulked at his call for an election - the first such demand by a major Ukrainian political figure since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
"I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections during this kind of war," Zelenskiy said.
Elections in war are prohibited by Ukrainian law. Analysts also say security concerns and the millions of Ukrainians abroad, under Russian occupation or fighting at the front mean it would be too difficult to hold an election.
ELECTIONS WOULD SPLIT UKRAINE, PRESIDENT SAYS
Zelenskiy's approval rating has remained generally stable at about 60%, but pollsters have said that while Ukrainians want fresh faces in politics, many have little appetite for voting now.
An August 5 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 57% of Ukrainians want elections only after fighting ends.
Echoing his previous comments on the matter, Zelenskiy said a wartime election might be possible if Kyiv's partners could guarantee security, but that no one has proposed such a plan.
"Elections right now are a tsunami for the state, which will split Ukraine," he said.
"That's why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an independent and sovereign state."
Fedorov, a longtime Zelenskiy ally who has been seen as a top political challenger, did not explicitly say whether he would stand in any future election. REUTERS

Singapore relaxes screening of dialect films after Dear You film spurs debate
Speaking at the National Day Rally, PM Lawrence Wong says the easing comes with the prerequisite that a Mandarin-dubbed version is available
“Even as we promote the use of Mandarin, we can also make more room for dialects,” said Wong, delivering his Mandarin speech at the annual National Day Rally. “Many see dialects as a cultural heritage worth preserving. I agree.”
Previously, guidelines dictated that Chinese films meant for theatrical release should generally be in Mandarin, and dialect films were allowed on a case-by-case basis. The policy was in line with Singapore’s Speak Mandarin Campaign, a movement launched in 1979 which originally aimed to replace dialects with Mandarin as the common language of Singapore’s Chinese community.
Wong recalled recent discourse sparked by Dear You, a Chinese indie production filmed primarily in Teochew which premiered locally in June.
“I believe it is because it reminded us of our pioneers, the sacrifices they made and the hardships they endured, as well as the values they lived by,” said Wong, adding that he had watched the Teochew version of the film.

Syria FM hopeful for security deal despite Israeli attacks

Breadcrumb
Syria foreign minister hopeful for security deal despite Israeli attacks
Israel has shown no willingness to sign a security agreement with Syria despite the two countries agreeing on "almost everything", Syria's foreign minister has said.
Speaking to Reuters days after Israel bombed a military base in northern Syria, Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks and that it was prepared to walk away from further talks.
"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it," Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
Washington has been trying to broker a security pact between President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government and Israel, which has occupied swathes of southwestern Syria and repeatedly bombed the country following the overthrow of the Assad regime.
Shaibani said that around the beginning of the year, the two sides had "agreed on paper to almost everything" regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after Assad's fall.
The deal would include several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and others where Syrian forces would deploy in varying degrees of force.
But he said Israel had avoided signing onto the deal, adding: "We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement."
Tensions over Syria rose on Tuesday when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase. It justified the attack by claiming that Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there, which Syria and Turkey have denied.
Negotiations uncertain
Shaibani said negotiations over the security agreement had been frozen since the start of the Iran war, but he expected them to restart. Contact between Syria and Israel was cut after the airbase strike, he said.
"Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force and it hasn’t succeeded" anywhere, Shaibani said. "I believe negotiations will resume soon."
No date has been set.
"The US is trying continuously to put pressure on Israel to return to the dialogue table," he added.
Asked how optimistic he was, Shaibani said: "It’s very hard to bet on Israel." But Syria had "very great hope" of building stable relationships with its neighbours.
"Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability.
Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948. Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in a 1967 war.
The priority now is to "stop Israeli aggression even before reaching a security agreement", Shaibani said. "Then perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan." US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said on Tuesday that Washington was working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkey and Syria.
Shaibani said there was no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he said must stop attacks and pave the way for the security deal rather than "entrenching ... Israeli occupation."
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Shaibani said Israel had bombed Abu al-Duhur even after Syria conveyed a message that it would not be a Turkish base.
Syria draws on Turkish support in military training and cooperation, he said, noting that this was also the case with Jordan, Saudi Arabia and others.
Damascus was thankful for Turkey’s support in rebuilding its military "and we won’t forgo support", he said.
(Reuters and TNA staff)

Kitesurfers ride pre-storm waves ahead of tempest making landfall
The impending arrival of Saturday's storm saw kitesurfers head out to catch the wind and the waves ahead of it making landfall.
At Lohusalu harbor west of Tallinn, enthusiasts said the pre-storm conditions were ideal for kitesurfing, also known as kiteboarding.
One of the hobbyists, Andrus, was already out at sea when the "Aktuaalne kaamera" crew arrived, and could be seen making jumps several meters high in the choppy waters.
Another, Tarmo, was still prepping his equipment. He had high hopes for a good session, but much depends on timing.
"Let's put it this way: when that rain cloud [points] gets here, the wind will get gusty. If it picks up enough before the rain cloud arrives and gets nice and strong, then you can definitely have a good session. Windy weather is good weather," Tarmo explained.
The whole season has been great, he said, with good winds since spring, while fall always brings windy weather and similarly suitable conditions, Tarmo went on.
Back out of the sea, Andrus said his pulse had raced a little higher than needed, and that he now needed a rest. "The adrenaline was pumping and it's been really cool," he said.
Andrus said he could have jumped higher, even as the wind had started to lull somewhat. He said he recommends kitesurfing to everyone. "It's a fever you can't get rid of," he noted.
As for safety, and avoiding a "kitemare," Andrus said: "If you can no longer hold onto the kite you see up there and it starts lifting you into the air without you doing anything, then it's dangerous. And usually, if there's sand on the beach and that sand starts flying, that's the first sign that you should be on the alert."
Saturday's storm came with a Level 2 warning and later picked up an intensity which would have kept even the most intrepid of kiteboarders on dry land. Felled branches and trees were seen and thousands of people were left without power.

'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system, with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.

60 years ago NASA took the first ever photo of Earth from the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:11:39 UTC
20:11:39 KST

In April, as the intrepid crew of Artemis II shot around the moon, NASA astronaut Christina Koch snapped a photograph of the distant Earth setting behind the lunar surface. It was an image with a 60-year-old legacy—one that often has been eclipsed by another famous photograph.
Koch’s picture drew instant comparison to the latter iconic image, “Earthrise,” a photograph shot by NASA astronaut Bill Anders during the Apollo 8 mission in December 1968. Like Artemis II, the Apollo 8 spaceflight looped around the moon—a crucial step on the road to NASA’s 1969 moon landing. But in truth, Koch’s image had an even earlier inspiration.
August 23 marks the anniversary of the first time Earth was photographed from the vicinity of the moon. The picture was taken on that date in 1966 by NASA’s Lunar Orbiter 1, the first U.S. spacecraft to ever orbit the moon.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Launched on August 10, Lunar Orbiter 1 was tasked with taking close-up pictures of the moon, in particular, nine possible landing sites for the upcoming Apollo missions. Over several days, it took hundreds of pictures covering more than five million square kilometers (two million square miles) of the lunar surface. Among those photos was a grainy black-and-white shot: in the foreground, it showed the rough terrain of the moon, pockmarked by craters, while in the background, it captured a semicircle of Earth, stark white against the inky black backdrop of space.
Without Lunar Orbiter 1, Anders might never have taken his iconic "Earthrise," seen below. Anders shot the picture on Christmas Eve in 1968.
Lunar Orbiter 1 was initially supposed to orbit the moon for a year, but that was not to be. After just months into its mission, NASA engineers determined the spacecraft’s condition had deteriorated beyond repair. In order to prevent any possible interference with the then upcoming Lunar Orbiter 2, NASA commanded it to crash into the farside of the moon during the vessel’s 577th orbit on October 29.
Still, looking at “Earthrise” and Koch’s “Earthset,” it is clear that Lunar Orbiter 1’s legacy lives on. While the missions get more elaborate, the sense of wonder at seeing our planet in space from our natural satellite hasn’t changed, despite the passing of 60 years.

How “thunderquakes” could help reveal hidden structures inside the Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:11:01 UTC
20:11:01 KST

When lightning strikes, it superheats the air around it and creates a shock wave that we hear as thunder. But thunder doesn’t just travel through the atmosphere to our ears.
When that energy reaches the ground, some of it is converted into seismic waves that ripple through the soil and rock beneath. The resulting vibrations are known as “thunderquakes.”
Until now, scientists haven’t understood these signals well enough to make practical use of them. Our team’s research shows that thunderquakes can be used to map the structure beneath the Earth’s subsurface—such as groundwater movement, environmental contamination, sinkholes, or for evaluating building sites and foundations—just like X-rays image inside the human body.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
We discovered this by listening to thunder with something found in communities around the world but unusual as a seismic measuring instrument: fiber-optic cable.
Turning fiber optics into vibration sensors
Using a technique called distributed acoustic sensing, we turned an ordinary fiber-optic cable, the kind used for internet or phone service, into a string of thousands of vibration sensors.
A laser-pulsing computer, called an interrogator, sends light through the cable and measures tiny changes caused by vibrations along its length. In our experiment, part of the Penn State FORESEE project, we used a cable that is over 2 miles (more than 4 kilometers) long. That gave us more than 2,100 sensors, spaced only a few feet apart, all listening to the ground at once.
Over two years, we used an old telecom fiber to record and identify 458 clear, high-quality thunderquakes.
The enormous amount of detail captured by this process has allowed us to see something that had been difficult to observe before: specific types of seismic waves produced when sound from the atmosphere interacts with the ground.
The most important of these seismic waves are what we call air-coupled Rayleigh waves. They are measurable at the surface but can be used to study the subsurface far below, even down 300 feet (around 100 meters).
How a thunderquake ‘X-rays’ the ground below
The trick to this technique is known as seismic dispersion: Waves of different frequencies travel at different depths. By measuring how the thunderquake’s wave speeds changed with frequency, we could reconstruct the seismic wave speed at different depths, which allows us to interpret the properties of the ground beneath the fiber.
The result was the equivalent of an X-ray of the subsurface extending roughly 300 feet underground, without drilling a single hole.
Imaging the subsurface typically requires specialized equipment, such as truck-mounted vibration sources or arrays of sensors that have to be installed for surveys. These approaches can be expensive and difficult to deploy over large areas.
Thunderstorms offer a naturally occurring source of seismic energy that is already spread across the landscape. And fiber-optic cables are buried beneath cities and towns around the world.
Instead of bringing a seismic source to the ground, we can listen to the storms passing overhead. That could eventually make it possible to monitor the shallow subsurface continuously, using infrastructure that is already in the ground and seismic energy that is already coming from the sky.
What we found at our test site
In State College, Pennsylvania, where we conducted the tests, the geology is mostly limestone and dolomite, rocks that can slowly dissolve as groundwater moves through them. Over time, this process creates fractures, caves and sinkholes.
Our thunderquake study revealed four distinct areas where seismic waves traveled much more slowly than through the surrounding rock. These “weak zones” could be caused by fractured or weathered rock or the presence of water or air. Two of them coincide with areas where satellite radar shows that the ground is actively subsiding. The depths of all four are consistent with fractures and voids documented at nearby sites.
These results matter because karst landscapes like the one beneath State College are widespread. They cover roughly 20 percent of the world’s continental land area and affect nearly a quarter of the global population. Sinkholes, groundwater contamination and other hazards associated with these landscapes can threaten buildings, infrastructure and public safety. Knowing where these hazards are allows for better construction and planning.
Not just for thunder, and not just on Earth
Our results demonstrate a fundamental process: Sound waves in the atmosphere can be converted into useful seismic waves in the solid Earth. But thunder is only one example.
Sonic booms, volcanic eruptions and meteor airbursts can produce similar atmospheric shock waves, potentially creating other natural seismic sources.
The idea may even extend beyond Earth. Earth-like tectonic earthquakes are not expected to be common on some other planets and moons, but atmospheric disturbances may still be present.
Titan, Saturn’s largest moon and the destination of NASA’s upcoming Dragonfly mission, is one intriguing possibility. If lightning and thunder occur there as models predict, atmospheric energy could potentially provide another way to investigate its subsurface.
Back on Earth, the atmosphere is constantly interacting with the ground beneath our feet. Our work suggests that this interaction could be a source of information about the hidden world below us.

"The FSB is blackmailing me": how Russian secret services tried to recruit a volunteer through his son, and why he decided to go to Moscow to save him
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:10:00 EEST
20:10:00 KST

"The FSB is blackmailing me": how Russian secret services tried to recruit a volunteer through his son, and why he decided to go to Moscow to save him
Mykhailo Puryshev, a volunteer who is well known in Ukraine for repeatedly travelling to besieged Mariupol to evacuate families, flew to Moscow of his own accord on 17 August 2026. He says he did so because he was being blackmailed: Russia's Federal Security Service, the FSB, had threatened to conscript his son into the Russian army and send him to fight against Ukraine unless Puryshev agreed to cooperate.
Shortly before his departure, Ukrainska Pravda managed to speak to some of Mykhailo's friends, and to Mykhailo himself. The volunteer was already outside Ukraine, in Poland, when our conversation took place. Here we tell his story in his own words.
It was the middle of summer 2026. The paperwork was almost complete. Mykhailo Puryshev, a serviceman who was close to being discharged, was doing household chores at his home on the outskirts of Kyiv. A year of military service was behind him, as were his health problems, although he was still feeling the effects of the two heart attacks he'd suffered. Just a few more documents to get hold of, and he could go back to volunteering.
Suddenly a call came through on Telegram. It was his son Oleksandr. Mykhailo hadn't seen him for more than four years. He was an adult now – 18. Mykhailo would probably have struggled to recognise him if they met. Oleksandr sounded anxious.
His son's frightened voice came down the phone. "Dad, there are some people here and they want to talk to you."
Mykhailo ended the call and rushed to find a second phone. Another call came through from his son's number. Mykhailo started recording. A man's voice came down the phone, speaking in Russian.
"Good afternoon, Mikhail [Mykhailo in Russian – ed.]. You understand who you're talking to. The equivalent of your 'security service'. Let's be friends, Mikhail. If you don't want to be friends… you help the military, don't you? How would you feel if your son were on the other side, up against those people? Who matters more to you, Mikhail?"
At first Mykhailo didn't know what to do. If they'd called from an unknown number, he could have sworn at them and hung up. But they were calling from his own son's number. That meant these people were with him and had him under their control. He had to figure out how to save him. How to save his son from the FSB.
Family in Russia and blackmail using his son
Mykhailo had divorced long before the full-scale invasion. His ex-wife took their two children – a son and a daughter – and moved to Russia. She had lived in Pskov since 2016. From time to time, his son would visit him in Mariupol. Father and son travelled around the country, ate hot dogs at petrol stations, stayed in good hotels and went to amusement parks. Oleksandr was interested in programming and computer games and dreamed of studying abroad. Russia's invasion changed everything.
Father and son began to talk less often. Mykhailo didn't want to put Oleksandr at risk unnecessarily because of his volunteer work. So Oleksandr was usually the one who called. He told his dad that the other kids at school didn't talk very nicely about Ukraine or Ukrainians. It seemed the invasion was forcing him to grow up too fast.
It was obvious that the Russians would draft his son into the army as soon as he turned 18. Mykhailo tried several times to get him out of Russia. First he attempted to enlist the help of his ex-wife: he tried to persuade her to sign some documents so that their son could fly to see Mykhailo's brother in Canada. But she refused. Then he tried to do it secretly, through acquaintances and friends. The plan almost worked, but at the last moment Oleksandr said he couldn't go through with it: if he fled to Canada, his mother would be very upset.
Then, on 16 July 2026, came the call mentioned at the start of this article.
The man from the "equivalent of the security service" who had suggested that they "be friends" was in fact issuing a direct ultimatum: either Mykhailo helped the Russians or his son would be sent to the front lines. Mykhailo was warned that if he tried to tell anyone about the conversation or attempted to get Oleksandr out of Russia with the help of relatives, the threats would quickly be carried out. But if their "friendship" worked out, they assured him they would help arrange Oleksandr's studies, possibly even abroad. They even promised to provide money for his education.
The Russian asked whether Mykhailo was in contact with his ex-wife and why their relationship was so strained. We do not know the details of Mykhailo's family life, but the man from the "equivalent of the security service" guaranteed that he could sort that out too. He promised that the next call would come from his ex-wife's number. They also said they wouldn't bother him too often: twice a month max.
"I felt dirty," Mykhailo recalled. "All sorts of ideas kept running through my head about how to sort this out. I cried. I wondered what to do. I was worried about my son, afraid they might have locked him up somewhere. He was frightened. Those people who'd come to see him weren't friends; they'd come to scare him. I think he was terrified."
The second time the Russians called, it was via Telegram from an unknown number, and they were excessively polite. Even when Mykhailo became emotional, they said calmly: "We're speaking to you politely, aren't we? And I know a lot about you. I respect you. And I'm speaking to you respectfully."
The unknown caller told Mykhailo to buy another phone and a new SIM card and to find a good hiding place for them. When the time came, he was to make contact.
The subsequent conversations, if they can be called that, became more specific: the Russians explained what they expected from the cooperation they were proposing. They wanted information about foreign military personnel serving in Ukraine's defence forces and the locations of various units. They were particularly interested in Azov.
"Has something happened to you? Why are you so sad? Why are you off social media? Why aren't you posting anything?" asked the unidentified caller who wanted to "be friends".
Mykhailo didn't know what to say. He couldn't swear at him. Nor could he directly refuse to cooperate. After all, the Russians were holding his son hostage. Mykhailo didn't know what had happened to him, where he was, or what conditions he was being held in. He didn't even know whether his son was free. The Russians desperately needed Mykhailo to go back to his volunteering and his social media as though nothing had happened.
"I've just gone through the military medical board and I'm waiting for the paperwork. I'm being discharged," Mykhailo explained. "And technically, I'm supposed to be at my permanent duty station. So just to avoid any questions, I'm staying at home, not really going anywhere, and I won't be posting anything until I have the documents."
The Russian kept asking when Mykhailo would be able to return to volunteering, because it was "very, very necessary" that he do so. This time, however, the conversation was more friendly than businesslike: the man from the "equivalent of the security service" seemed to have changed tactics and was trying to act more casually, asking about the weather, Mykhailo's health, relationships, women. And, almost in passing, he asked where Mykhailo's unit was currently stationed.
Mykhailo gave a vague answer: "Somewhere in the east."
There were five calls in total. It was becoming clear that the Russians were losing patience and were no longer prepared to believe that the military medical board bureaucracy could take so long. They demanded that Mykhailo go back to his volunteering and finally begin cooperating with them.
The last conversation took place on 3 August. After that, they communicated only by text. Mykhailo even deleted the text messages to make it look as if he really was interested in cooperating with the Russians.
The decision
Meanwhile, a plan was taking shape in his mind. Mykhailo spoke to various people who suggested different ways of resolving the situation, including physically getting Oleksandr out of Russia.
But putting other people's lives at risk was unacceptable to the volunteer, as was forcing his son to take such a risk. Mykhailo decided to fly to Moscow and sort it out once and for all.
"Everyone's worried about whether I'll be all right. But if someone else got my son out, wouldn't they have a family too? Of course they would. This is my problem. I've tried to solve it. There is no option in which no one suffers. This is my child – I can take responsibility for him myself. I believe this is the best option there is," Mykhailo explained.
All this time he kept on trying to contact his son, but there was no answer. Then, around the beginning of August, his ex-wife called relatives and repeatedly urged them to tell Mykhailo not to try to contact Oleksandr.
The unknown Russian man who had "wanted to be friends" kept promising to arrange a conversation with Mykhailo's son. At one point he even suggested meeting in person, saying that Mykhailo could travel to Russia via a third country such as Kazakhstan. To convince him that he had the necessary connections, the man even promised to make sure that no stamp showing that Mykhailo had crossed into Russia would be put in his passport. But Mykhailo never once got to hear his son's voice.
"It was difficult," he said. "I considered different ways of solving the problem. Some of them wouldn't have been ideal for me. How long can someone who's had two heart attacks survive in captivity? Not long, I don't think. But there is hope that perhaps things will turn out differently.
I always say that wherever I've been and whatever I've done, I've always put my faith in God. Because there was no logic to any of it. Let them do whatever they want. My son will stop being of interest to them. There'll be no one left to blackmail me with, and nothing to blackmail me over. There will be no reason to waste resources."
Eventually Mykhailo travelled to Poland and on to Türkiye. On the Turkish coast, he bought a plane ticket to Sheremetyevo airport in Moscow. His plan was to arrive at the airport and be detained at passport control.
"I've left a video explaining everything. I wanted people to understand me. Parents will understand why I did this. If they're decent, proper parents, borders won't matter to them. Parents will go and get their children, whatever the cost," Mykhailo said.
He said that just before the flight, he'd finally felt a sense of relief. Suddenly he remembered how much he'd loved swimming in the river as a child. He used to jump in off a dam. It was incredibly scary. But once you'd taken that step, there was no way back. All you could do was plunge into the water and swim...
From entrepreneur to volunteer
We can't know exactly what Mykhailo was feeling at that moment. But he certainly knew who he would be dealing with and what those people are capable of. After all, he had first-hand experience of dealing with Russian occupying forces in Mariupol in 2022.
The Russians were interested in Mykhailo Puryshev for a reason. He was one of the few volunteers who had managed to get into Mariupol during the occupation and evacuate people. He later continued helping civilians evacuate from frontline cities, including Kherson.
Before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mykhailo did not consider himself a volunteer. He lived in the city and ran several businesses, including an IT company and a nightclub. On 24 February 2022, he took his family and relatives to safety in Ukraine's west, bought a red Mercedes minibus, painted "Volunteer" all over it and drove back to Mariupol. He managed to get into the city on 8 March. He was lucky: at the time, he didn't understand the immensity of the risks he was about to face.
Mykhailo made six trips to Mariupol in all. He brought aid into the city in his red minibus, and on the return journey he took families with children out. There were no humanitarian corridors, so attacks would be going on during the evacuations.
On subsequent trips, other people Mykhailo knew also went with him in their own vehicles, which meant they could rescue more people. By his estimate, around a thousand Mariupol residents were rescued during the spring of 2022. The volunteer's trips were reported on by Ukrainian and international media outlets, including Euronews, Fox News, CNN, the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne, 1+1, NV and local outlet Mrpl.city.
Getting through the Russian checkpoints wasn't easy. The Russian occupying forces thought Mykhailo was either insane or a spy. They would search his vehicle thoroughly. Eventually they began to recognise him. They thought he would either be killed by Russian artillery or accidentally shot by his own side. During one of his trips, a shell landed near his minibus, damaging the bonnet and blowing out one of the side doors.
His final trip to Mariupol was in May. Mykhailo had learned that there might be children inside the Azovstal steelworks, so he decided to try to rescue them. He took two megaphones in addition to his usual humanitarian supplies. He planned to drive around the plant and broadcast a recorded message offering evacuation. Mykhailo hoped that by doing this, he would be able to locate civilians who were sheltering from the constant bombardment alongside the Ukrainian troops.
This time, however, he failed to reach the city. During his previous trip he had been threatened by so-called militants from the "DPR" (the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic) at one of the checkpoints. They said that if they saw his Mercedes again, they would put him in a basement and either keep him prisoner or shoot him.
Mykhailo was detained at a checkpoint near Mariupol. His vehicle was confiscated and he was taken away for interrogation. There were a lot of people in the building where he was held. They were all taken away to be interrogated. They were tortured too. Electric shock was the main method.
There was one incident that Mykhailo is unlikely ever to forget. One of the prisoners was tortured so brutally that he could literally no longer walk. He was dragged bodily into the room.
"The guy had left the room on his own two feet, but when he came back, they had to drag him in," Mykhailo recalls. "People immediately started looking for ways to help him, searching for painkillers. The stench of burnt skin was overwhelming – they'd subjected him to such severe electric shocks. It felt as though human life meant absolutely nothing there."
But the collaborators were the most brutal. At times they were even more vicious than the Russians. In their eagerness to prove themselves useful to the Russian occupying forces, they could torture prisoners in an attempt to extract information that did not even exist.
The Russians laughed at Mykhailo's determination to reach Azovstal. When they realised that he was completely serious, they asked him how he could possibly imagine doing it. Eventually, during one of the interrogations, Mykhailo was released. The Russians even returned the red minibus he'd arrived in. On the way to Zaporizhzhia, he managed to evacuate two more families with children. He called the other volunteers and advised them not to travel to the city any more: it was becoming too dangerous.
But that wasn't the end of his volunteer work. Mykhailo spent some time delivering humanitarian aid to Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts after they had been liberated. During one of his trips to Kramatorsk, he came up with the idea of setting up invincibility centres – heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist people facing hardships due to power cuts – for both military personnel and civilians. Water was a major problem in frontline cities: people had been unable to wash properly for months.
The first invincibility centre was established in Bakhmut. A well was drilled in a basement, and a filtration system enabled up to 1,000 litres of water an hour to be pumped through it. People started coming to the pink basement – Mykhailo and the other volunteers painted the centres pink – to wash themselves, do their laundry, or pick up toys that the volunteers had left there for the children.
This was also how they found families with children who were reluctant to leave. Mykhailo and his friends would keep track of them and try to persuade them to evacuate. Sometimes they succeeded. Similar invincibility centres were later established in Avdiivka, Vuhledar, Kupiansk, Druzhkivka, Kostiantynivka, Kherson and Huliaipole. The most expensive one cost just over half a million hryvnias (about US$11,100). Eventually the Russians began bombing the centres. They claimed on Russian television that the volunteers were "helping the Nazis".
The volunteers suspected that local collaborators were helping the Russians locate the basements equipped for washing and doing laundry, as they would enter the premises and film them. They managed to catch one of these "helpers" red-handed, and several others were caught later.
Mykhailo officially registered his volunteer organisation, naming it Unity of People. Some members of the team decided to enlist in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and he joined them. He wanted to keep an eye on his friends.
But after suffering two heart attacks and related health issues, Mykhailo was deemed unfit for military service – he was having to take four different medications every day to keep his condition under control. He returned to his home near Kyiv, where he was finishing up the paperwork and planning his next volunteer projects, when on 16 July, he received that phone call from the FSB.
***
Mykhailo Puryshev landed at Sheremetyevo on the morning of 17 August. He has not been in contact with anyone since. His friends have no information about what has happened to him.
Videos continue to appear on Mykhailo's social media accounts, but he said that his team would handle all communication from then on.
- -
P.S. Ukrainska Pravda has contacted human rights advocates who are aware of Puryshev's situation and are trying to find ways to help him.
UP also requested comment from the Security Service of Ukraine, but had not received a response at the time this article was posted.
P.P.S. During our conversations with Mykhailo and his friends, we expressed concern about his decision and warned him about the possible risks. However, it was clear from our conversations that unfortunately, Mykhailo was not going to change his plans.
Stanislav Kozliuk and Yevhen Buderatskyi

Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists, as reported by Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne
Details: Zelenskyy was commenting on corruption cases involving former representatives of the President's Office, including its former deputy head, Iryna Mudra.
The president said he has no information on these cases beyond what is already publicly known.
Quote: "There was enough detail to dismiss her. I heard, essentially at the same time as everyone else, about certain conversations regarding actions – real or potential.
